How Risky Is Your Data-Driven Policy?

Omar Besbes    Alon Rieger
Abstract

Data-driven algorithms are ubiquitous across industries, and there is an extensive literature on analyzing their average performance. The risk profile of such algorithms, while critical, is much less understood. This paper quantifies the risk of data-driven policies and isolates its sources. We evaluate a policy through the conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) of its loss over the training sample, any policy randomization, and the future outcome, at a fixed unknown distribution. Regret against an oracle that knows the distribution decomposes into expected post-sample regret (PS), the average outcome-only CVaR gap of the selected action, and a sample-risk premium (SR), the additional tail risk omitted by averaging those evaluations. The analogous premium vanishes under expected loss.

We characterize when the premium vanishes and how large it is relative to post-sample regret. For losses with a continuous density near the tail cutoff, we identify conditions under which both components decay at the same rate, yet the limiting ratio of the premium to post-sample regret can reach the thousands. When a probability mass at the cutoff moves with the action, the premium can decay more slowly and dominate post-sample regret. We establish conditions under which sample average approximation learns the oracle action at rate n−1/2n^{-1/2} in both settings, but its combined-risk regret is of order n−1n^{-1} in the first and n−1/2n^{-1/2} in the second. In finite-sample numerical examples of SAA in both settings, the premium accounts for approximately 74%74\%–97%97\% of regret.

keywords: data-driven decisions, conditional value-at-risk, sample average approximation, regret decomposition

1 Introduction

Data-driven decision procedures are now deployed at scale. A retailer fits an order quantity to last year’s sales for each of thousands of products; a cloud provider sizes capacity from recent usage; an insurer sets a retention from a window of historical claims. Each procedure is retrained and redeployed many times, and in each deployment the realized loss depends on two things: the data the procedure was trained on, and the outcome it then faces. Under an expected-loss objective, averaging performance conditional on the training sample recovers the overall expected loss. Under a tail-risk objective, averaging conditional risk evaluations need not recover the risk of the learning procedure. We ask how large this difference can be and when it becomes a leading component of regret.

Tail risk is the natural criterion when the costly events are rare: a stockout that loses a customer, a capacity shortfall that breaches a service level, a reserve that falls short of a claim. Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR), the average loss in the worst (1−δ)(1-\delta) fraction of cases, is a standard expression of that criterion. When the distribution of the outcome is known, the risk-averse problem is well understood. The action is fixed in advance, and the only way to be unlucky is to draw a bad outcome.

Learning the action from a finite sample changes what unlucky means. In the retailer’s case, a slow year produces a low order, and an ordinary week then arrives as a stockout. The demand was not unusual; the sample was. Conversely, a week of unusually high demand does little harm when the sample ran high as well and the order already covers it. For a learned policy, large losses can reflect a mismatch between the sample that chose the action and the outcome that tests it, and any randomization inside the policy is one more draw of the same kind. If risk means being unlucky, the unlucky event is the combined draw of the sample, any randomization, and the future outcome. We call the CVaR of the loss over that combined draw the combined-risk CVaR, following the total CVaR of Lu et al. (2015). It is what a practitioner estimates by pooling realized losses across deployments, as opposed to the within-deployment CVaR of the action a particular sample happened to produce.

The question becomes precise once the regret is split. The regret of a learning policy against an oracle that knows the distribution is the sum of two nonnegative pieces. The first is the expected post-sample regret: the gap between the outcome-only CVaR of the selected action and the oracle value, averaged over samples and any policy randomization. This component already captures the effect of learning on the quality of the selected action. It is the quantity that most of the data-driven optimization literature studies. The second is a sample-risk premium: the difference between combined-risk CVaR and the average outcome-only CVaR of the selected actions. The analogous premium is zero under an expected-loss criterion. Under CVaR, it can dominate regret even when the selected actions are nearly optimal. The premium can be the whole of the regret. Section 3 gives a two-action example in which every action the policy returns is optimal, so expected post-sample regret is zero, while the combined-risk evaluation still pays a strictly positive premium. The training sample selects different actions on different draws.

Three questions organize the paper. When is the premium zero, and what exactly is charged when it is not? How do the two pieces scale with the sample size, and which features of the loss, the distribution, and the policy set their relative order? And how does the standard policy, sample average approximation, fare under the combined criterion? Each question is about the learning procedure rather than about any one action it produces. The usual assessment of a data-driven policy fixes the sample and evaluates the action it induced; that assessment sees the first piece and not the second. We answer the three questions for a general loss and a scalar action, at a fixed unknown distribution with no parametric family and no prior.

1.1 Main contributions

Quantifying the sample-risk premium. Building on total CVaR and known conditional-risk comparisons, discussed in Section 1.2, we quantify the premium relative to oracle regret for scalar decisions under a general loss, derive its sharp smooth and atomic expansions, and establish the resulting regret rates for sample average approximation. The premium measures the additional tail risk from evaluating those losses together, under one threshold shared across samples, beyond the average risk of the selected actions. It vanishes exactly when there is a threshold that minimizes the variational objective for almost every selected action, and therefore when the action is fixed; under expectation the analogous premium vanishes for every policy. The expected post-sample regret vanishes when the returned action is an oracle action. A nonasymptotic upper bound relates the premium to the dispersion of the induced loss cutoffs. The local results below then identify when the premium is comparable to, dominates, or persists beyond post-sample regret.

The order and magnitude of each component. We determine how the two pieces scale with the sample size, and which features of the loss, the distribution, and the policy set their relative order. We characterize four representative regimes at a fixed distribution, under their respective regularity and policy-concentration conditions. The smooth regime is the one in which the cutoff moves to first order with the action and the loss has a density there. Both components are then of order rn2r_{n}^{2} when the action concentrates at rate rnr_{n}. The premium is an additional variance penalty: a common tail threshold across samples gives a larger local action curvature than a threshold re-optimized for each selected action. The ratio of these curvatures is 1+K1+K. For centered limiting fluctuations, the ratio of the premium to expected post-sample regret tends to KK. For squared loss with lognormal outcomes, Table 1 gives K≈3900K\approx 3900 at δ=0.99\delta=0.99 and K≈50000K\approx 50000 at δ=0.999\delta=0.999. These are asymptotic coefficients; they do not specify the premium at a given sample size. The atomic regime is the one in which an atom sits at the cutoff and moves with the action, and there the expected post-sample regret is of order rn2r_{n}^{2} and the premium is of order rnr_{n}. The mixing regime is the one in which the policy keeps visiting several optimal actions with no common minimizing threshold, and there the premium tends to a positive constant. The displaced regime is the one in which the policy stays off a unique well-separated optimum, and there the expected post-sample regret is bounded away from zero.

Sample average approximation. Under the conditions of Proposition 4.2, SAA learns the oracle action at rate n−1/2n^{-1/2} in both regimes. Nevertheless, its combined-risk regret is Θ⁡(n−1)\Theta(n^{-1}) in the smooth regime and Θ(n−1/2)\Theta(n^{-1/2}) in the atomic regime, where the premium dominates. We identify the limiting variance of the action and the resulting atomic premium constant. Finite-sample examples show that the premium accounts for most regret in both regimes: Monte Carlo estimates give shares of about 74%74\%–94%94\% in bounded smooth squared-loss examples, while calculations from the exact distribution of the uniform-demand newsvendor order give shares of 76%76\% at n=110n=110 and 95%95\% at n=1630n=1630. These results show why the action’s learning rate alone does not describe the policy’s tail-risk performance.

1.2 Related literature

Coherent risk measures (Artzner et al. 1999) and the variational representation of CVaR (Rockafellar and Uryasev 2002) are the language of the papers below. The closest connections concern total-CVaR and risk estimation, conditional-risk and quantile-score decompositions, Bayesian and contextual risk, and empirical optimization.

The total-CVaR perspective.

A plug-in evaluation treats the estimated distribution as known, so the risk it reports is the risk of the future outcome alone. The papers below bring the risk contributed by the data into the evaluation. Lu et al. (2015) do so by changing the objective. Under the name total CVaR, they apply CVaR to the profit of the historical sample and next-period demand taken together, explicitly contrast that criterion with expected conditional CVaR, and optimize operational statistics for it, for a repeated newsvendor with parametric location-scale demand. Building on this criterion, we compare the sample-risk premium with oracle regret for scalar decisions under a general loss, derive its smooth and atomic expansions, and establish the resulting regret rates for sample average approximation.

Pitera and Schmidt (2018) show that plug-in estimators of value-at-risk and expected shortfall can underestimate risk. They correct it by an acceptance criterion: the reported position has to be acceptable as a risk capital. Francioni and Herzog (2012) require that the next observation exceed the estimated quantile with the nominal probability, for every value of the parameter. The quantile of the fitted distribution fails that requirement, and for the normal distribution a distortion that uses the sampling distribution of the estimate restores it. Gerrard and Tsanakas (2011) study how often a threshold set to a nominal tail probability fails, as in a capital or inventory rule. Parameter error can raise that frequency. For increasing transformations of location-scale families the frequency can be computed without knowing the true parameter. A tighter nominal level for the plug-in threshold and a threshold taken from the Bayesian predictive distribution both achieve a prescribed failure probability; under the prior proportional to 1/σ1/\sigma, the predictive threshold meets the nominal level exactly. Bignozzi and Tsanakas (2016) subtract the estimated capital from the loss and measure the risk that remains. That remainder is the further capital that makes the position acceptable. Rules based on the parametric bootstrap and on the predictive distribution reduce it, and for location-scale families a capital estimator can remove it.

The risk-estimation papers above calibrate data-dependent capital, quantile, or threshold rules to a nominal standard, accounting for sampling randomness in that calibration. Our analysis uses the regret decomposition to quantify how much of the excess risk comes from the premium, including when the selected actions approach an oracle action.

The premium also differs from the optimizer’s curse: selection using noisy value estimates can make the selected alternative’s estimated performance optimistic (Smith and Winkler 2006). Here the premium is a difference between true population risk evaluations of a policy, and can be positive even when every selected action is optimal.

Conditional risk and quantile-score decompositions.

The nonnegativity of the premium follows from known conditional-risk comparisons. For a coherent distortion risk measure, the risk of an outcome is at least the average of the risks computed after extra information (Iancu et al. 2015). Expected shortfall has the same property because it is concave under mixtures (Embrechts et al. 2021, Pertaia and Uryasev 2019, Tselishchev 2019), and the same comparison follows for optimized certainty equivalents from their infimum-of-expectations representation, under the required integrability conditions (Ben-Tal and Teboulle 2007). Taking the information to be the action makes the difference the premium. The same difference is (1−δ)−1(1-\delta)^{-1} times the resolution term of a quantile score, the gain from letting the cutoff depend on side information (Bentzien and Friederichs 2014, Ehm and Ovcharov 2017, Pohle 2020). For a fixed policy, this identity follows by taking its realized loss as the forecast target, its action as side information, and the standard pinball loss as the quantile score. The local behavior of quantile-score excess, including quadratic and linear growth under different distributional conditions, is also studied in Steinwart and Christmann (2011). Our analysis relates the premium to the movement of the loss cutoff, the curvature of the outcome-only objective, and the dispersion of the learned action. Comparing it with post-sample regret yields the smooth and atomic orders and the coefficient KK under the respective regularity conditions. The mixing regime further identifies when the premium remains positive as post-sample regret vanishes.

Composite and Bayesian risk.

Bayesian approaches condition on the observed sample and represent uncertainty about the outcome distribution through a posterior. Some apply an outer risk measure to a parameter-dependent performance criterion; others evaluate risk under the posterior predictive distribution of future outcomes. These constructions differ in how they aggregate parameter and outcome uncertainty.

Qian et al. (2019) nest two risk measures. The inner measure prices the decision when the parameter of the outcome distribution is known. The outer measure prices the fact that the parameter must be estimated. Stochastic programming, robust optimization, and distributionally robust optimization are the cases in which one of the two measures is an expectation or a worst-case value. Lin et al. (2022b) apply a risk functional, nested over the Bayesian posterior of an unknown transition distribution, to the expected total cost of a finite-horizon Markov decision process, and solve the CVaR case by an approximate dynamic program. Ma et al. (2026) use the same nesting for stochastic control: the inner risk is conditional on a latent environment parameter, the outer risk is taken under the posterior, and the action may depend on that posterior. Bodnar et al. (2020), Bodnar et al. (2022) and Kim and Kang (2021) compute portfolio value-at-risk and CVaR from the posterior predictive distribution of returns, so the allocation is a function of the observed sample. Jaiswal et al. (2023) replace the expectation in the Bayes risk by an entropic risk over the posterior and give rates for the approximate posterior and for the decision, with the newsvendor among the examples. Sadatsafavi et al. (2022) measure the value of a larger development sample by the net-benefit gap between the predictions of a fitted risk model and the correct predictions.

Our evaluation takes a frequentist perspective before the sample is observed. The distribution FF is fixed and unknown, and no prior is placed on it. Combined-risk CVaR is the tail risk of the loss under the combined draw of the sample given FF, the action that sample induces, and the future outcome. The distinction is in the conditioning: posterior and predictive evaluations condition on the observed sample, whereas combined-risk CVaR evaluates repeated draws of the sample and the future outcome at the same fixed FF. It is distinct from the nested value that first replaces each action by its outcome-only CVaR and then takes the tail of that number: either one can be larger.

Contextual risk.

Tao et al. (2025) study when a nested assessment of contextual and outcome uncertainty agrees with one risk evaluation of the two sources taken together. Their revised analysis also considers integrated learning and optimization. Here the information is a training sample, independent of the future outcome at a fixed FF, and the distribution of the learned action changes with the sample size. Our focus is on regret against a distribution-knowing oracle and on how its post-sample and sample-risk components compare as the sample grows.

Outcome-only empirical optimization.

A large literature approximates an unknown distribution by the sample and then evaluates risk on future outcomes only. Sampling variability enters as estimation error. For CVaR objectives, Meng et al. (2010) show that under continuous distributions, sample-average optimal values converge to the population optimum and limit points of sample-average stationary points are stationary for the true problem. Shapiro (2013) shows that, under mild moment and regularity conditions, limit points of sample-average solutions lie in the set of outcome-only optima. Dentcheva et al. (2017) and Guigues et al. (2018) refine this analysis with limit theorems for the estimation error, and Banholzer et al. (2022) give rates of convergence in mean under Lipschitz and moment conditions. Data-driven inventory applications include expected-profit optimization with an empirical value-at-risk constraint (Lin et al. 2022a), support-vector formulations of CVaR newsvendor criteria (Chen 2024), a feature-based CVaR newsvendor (Liu and Zhu 2024), and high-probability near-optimality guarantees for risk-averse multiperiod inventory (Jiang et al. 2026). Across this literature, the guarantees concern an optimizer of an outcome-only risk. Lee et al. (2020) give high-probability excess population-risk guarantees for empirical optimized-certainty-equivalent minimization, including CVaR, while Soma and Yoshida (2020) directly bound expected excess population CVaR. These results control the post-sample component, directly or after averaging over training samples. Such guarantees account for sampling variability through the population risk of the selected action. They do not by themselves characterize the additional sample-risk premium, which can determine the order of combined-risk regret. Our SAA analysis connects the concentration of the learned action to the rates of both components.

Related work studies the distribution of cumulative regret in sequential learning. Fan and Glynn (2025) and Simchi-Levi et al. (2025) show how expected-regret performance can conceal substantial tail risk arising from the learning process. Here we study the loss of a learned action on an independent future outcome and decompose its combined-risk CVaR regret into expected post-sample regret and a sample-risk premium.

The companion paper (Besbes and Rieger 2026) specializes the decomposition and the asymptotic regimes developed here to the newsvendor. It studies worst-case regret over bounded demand distributions and optimizes policies within a class based on order statistics. For every fixed δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), the minimax rate over all data-driven policies is Θ(n−1/4)\Theta(n^{-1/4}), while at δ=0\delta=0 it is Θ(n−1/2)\Theta(n^{-1/2}), and uniform windows of width n3/4n^{3/4} attain the rate Θ(n−1/4)\Theta(n^{-1/4}). The present paper develops the structural and local asymptotic analysis for a general loss at a fixed distribution.

2 Problem Formulation

We consider a stochastic optimization problem with a nonempty Borel action set 𝒳⊆ℝ\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}. The decision maker chooses x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} before a random outcome ξ∈ℝ\xi\in\mathbb{R} is realized. We use c⁡(x,ξ)c(x,\xi) to denote the loss incurred by the decision maker.

CVaR.

We adopt Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) as our performance criterion, a tail-risk measure that focuses on large losses.

Definition 2.1 (CVaR).

For δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1) and an integrable random variable XX with CDF FXF_{X}, define

CVaRδ​[X]=11−δ⋅∫δ1FX−1​(u)​𝑑u.\text{CVaR}_{\delta}[X]\penalty\ \penalty\ =\penalty\ \penalty\ \frac{1}{1-\delta}\cdot\int_{\delta}^{1}F_{X}^{-1}\left(u\right)\,du\ . (2.1)

Here, FX−1​(u)=inf{y:FX​(y)≥u}F_{X}^{-1}(u)=\inf\{y:F_{X}(y)\geq u\} is the ut​hu^{th} quantile of XX.

The Value-at-Risk at level δ\delta, denoted by VaRδ​[X]\mathrm{VaR}_{\delta}[X], is the corresponding quantile,

VaRδ​[X]:=FX−1​(δ).\mathrm{VaR}_{\delta}[X]:=F_{X}^{-1}(\delta).

Equivalently, it is the smallest loss threshold tt such that ℙ⁡(X≤t)≥δ\mathbb{P}(X\leq t)\geq\delta.

Throughout, δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1). The excluded endpoint δ=0\delta=0 is the risk-neutral case, CVaR0​[X]=𝔼​[X]\text{CVaR}_{0}[X]=\mathbb{E}[X], in which the criterion is the expectation and the premium studied below vanishes identically by the tower property.

Informally, CVaR is the expected loss conditional on the loss lying in the worst (1−δ)(1-\delta)-tail of its distribution. When the distribution has no probability mass at the δt​h\delta^{th} quantile, CVaR admits the following commonly studied expression CVaRδ​[X]=𝔼⁡[X∣X≥FX−1​(δ)]\text{CVaR}_{\delta}[X]=\mathbb{E}[X\mid X\geq F_{X}^{-1}\left(\delta\right)]. When there is an atom at the cutoff, the definition includes only the fraction of that atom needed to obtain a tail of probability 1−δ1-\delta.

An equivalent representation of CVaR was shown by Rockafellar and Uryasev (2002, Theorem 10):

CVaRδ​[X]=inft∈ℝ{t+11−δ⋅𝔼⁡[(X−t)+]}.\text{CVaR}_{\delta}[X]\penalty\ \penalty\ =\penalty\ \penalty\ \inf_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\left\{t+\frac{1}{1-\delta}\cdot\mathbb{E}\left[\left(X-t\right)^{+}\right]\right\}\ . (2.2)

We call that threshold the cutoff of the loss, and the cutoff of an action xx is the cutoff of c⁡(x,ξ)c(x,\xi).

The same representation applies when the loss is generated by a random action. Below we evaluate it over the training sample, any policy randomization, and the future outcome together.

Data and policies.

In the present paper, we consider the case in which the distribution FF is unknown to the decision maker, but the decision maker has access to nn i.i.d. samples ξ1n:=(ξ1,…,ξn)\xi_{1}^{n}:=(\xi_{1},\ldots,\xi_{n}) from FF. We consider a class Π\Pi of data-driven policies, each a measurable probability kernel from ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} to 𝒳\mathcal{X}. A policy maps the sample to a distribution in 𝒫⁡(𝒳)\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X}), the set of probability distributions on 𝒳\mathcal{X}. We suppress dependence on nn in the policy notation. In particular, a policy π∈Π\pi\in\Pi specifies

π:ξ1n↦Hξ1n,\pi:\xi_{1}^{n}\mapsto H_{\xi_{1}^{n}}\ ,

where Hξ1n∈𝒫⁡(𝒳)H_{\xi_{1}^{n}}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X}) is the distribution of the action conditional on the sample. For an observed sample ξ1n\xi_{1}^{n}, the distribution π⁡(ξ1n)\pi(\xi_{1}^{n}) specifies a possibly randomized action. We identify a deterministic policy with the point mass at its prescribed action. Note that even for a deterministic policy, the resulting decision xπx^{\pi} is a random variable because it depends on the random sample ξ1n\xi_{1}^{n}. The decision maker commits to the policy before observing the sample.

We let ξ1n∼F\xi_{1}^{n}\sim F generate the sample, xπ∼π⁡(ξ1n)x^{\pi}\sim\pi(\xi_{1}^{n}) denote the resulting decision, and ξ∼F\xi\sim F denote the future outcome realization, drawn independently of the sample and of any randomization in the policy; the induced loss random variable is c⁡(xπ,ξ)c(x^{\pi},\xi).

In this notation the oracle value is OPTδ​(F)=infx∈𝒳QF​(x)\text{OPT}_{\delta}(F)=\inf_{x\in\mathcal{X}}Q_{F}\!\left(x\right), and whenever this infimum is attained we write xF∗x^{*}_{F} for an optimal action. We state xF∗x^{*}_{F} with the subscript when it matters for the understanding, and otherwise write x∗x^{*}. Proposition 3.9 treats the case of several optimal actions.

In contrast to the oracle, the data-driven setting carries two layers of randomness: the sample ξ1n\xi_{1}^{n}, which feeds into the action xπx^{\pi}, and the independent future outcome ξ\xi, both governed by FF. Following the total-CVaR perspective of Lu et al. (2015), expressed there as lower-tail CVaR of profit, we evaluate upper-tail CVaR of loss over both sources of randomness. The tail-risk value of a policy under FF is therefore

CVaRδ​[c⁡(xπ,ξ)]:=inft∈ℝ{t+11−δ⋅𝔼ξ1n∼F,xπ∼π⁡(ξ1n),ξ∼F​[(c⁡(xπ,ξ)−t)+]}.\text{CVaR}_{\delta}[c\left(x^{\pi},\xi\right)]\penalty\ :=\penalty\ \inf_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\left\{t+\frac{1}{1-\delta}\cdot\mathbb{E}_{\xi_{1}^{n}\sim F,x^{\pi}\sim\pi(\xi_{1}^{n}),\xi\sim F}\left[\left(c\left(x^{\pi},\xi\right)-t\right)^{+}\right]\right\}\ . (2.5)

Throughout the paper, CVaRδ​[⋅]\text{CVaR}_{\delta}[\cdot] without a distribution subscript denotes evaluation over the combined randomness of sample, policy, and outcome; outcome-only evaluation at a fixed action is written CVaRδ,ξ∼F​[⋅]\text{CVaR}_{\delta,\xi\sim F}[\cdot], equivalently QF​(⋅)Q_{F}\!\left(\cdot\right).

Lipschitz condition.

Assumption 2.2 is in force throughout. The smooth and atomic results in Section 3 use, in addition, the following Lipschitz condition. There is a nonnegative random variable L⁡(ξ)L(\xi) with 𝔼⁡[L⁡(ξ)]<∞\mathbb{E}[L(\xi)]<\infty such that

|c⁡(x,ξ)−c⁡(y,ξ)|≤L⁡(ξ)​|x−y|\bigl|c(x,\xi)-c(y,\xi)\bigr|\penalty\ \penalty\ \leq\penalty\ \penalty\ L(\xi)\,|x-y| (2.6)

for FF-almost every ξ\xi, simultaneously for all x,y∈𝒳x,y\in\mathcal{X}. Additional moment and regularity conditions are stated with the relevant results. The SAA results in Section 4 use their own stated assumptions.11 1 Joint measurability makes x↦ϕF​(x,t)x\mapsto\phi_{F}\!\left(x,t\right) measurable for each tt. Since t↦ϕF​(x,t)t\mapsto\phi_{F}\!\left(x,t\right) is finite and convex, hence continuous, its infimum over ℝ\mathbb{R} agrees with the infimum over ℚ\mathbb{Q}, so QF​(⋅)Q_{F}\!\left(\cdot\right) is measurable, and the outcome-only CVaR of the induced action is a random variable.

We define the regret of a data-driven policy as the nonnegative difference between the CVaR induced by the policy and the oracle value OPTδ​(F)\text{OPT}_{\delta}(F) when the distribution is known

ℛδ,n​(π,F)=CVaRδ​[c⁡(xπ,ξ)]−OPTδ​(F).\mathcal{R}_{\delta,n}\left(\pi,F\right)\penalty\ \penalty\ =\penalty\ \penalty\ \text{CVaR}_{\delta}[c\left(x^{\pi},\xi\right)]-{\text{OPT}_{\delta}(F)}\ . (2.7)

Nonnegativity follows from the comparison in Section 3. This regret evaluates the learning procedure before the sample and any policy randomization are realized. The tail of the combined loss depends on both the sample-induced action and the future outcome, which remain independent. Variation across samples can increase combined-risk CVaR even when every selected action is optimal under its outcome-only CVaR.

For an operational interpretation, consider independent deployments under the same distribution FF and policy π\pi, with the sample size nn fixed. Each deployment draws a fresh training sample, selects an action, and records the loss from an independent future outcome. As the number of deployments grows, the empirical CVaR of these losses converges to the combined-risk value in equation (2.5). If instead the realized sample and action are held fixed and outcomes are independently redrawn from FF, the empirical CVaR converges to the outcome-only value QF​(xπ)Q_{F}\!\left(x^{\pi}\right).

3 Decomposition of combined-risk regret

After the sample is observed and the policy has selected an action, one may instead evaluate tail risk only over the future realization. Fix π∈Π\pi\in\Pi. Independence of the future outcome gives the post-sample outcome-only CVaR Ψnπ=QF​(xπ)\Psi_{n}^{\pi}=Q_{F}\!\left(x^{\pi}\right), with conditional variational representation

Ψnπ:=inft∈ℝ{t+11−δ𝔼ξ∼F[(c(xπ,ξ)−t)+|ξ1n,xπ]}.\Psi_{n}^{\pi}\penalty\ :=\penalty\ \inf_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\left\{t+\frac{1}{1-\delta}\,\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim F}\!\left[\left.\left(c\left(x^{\pi},\xi\right)-t\right)^{+}\,\right|\,\xi_{1}^{n},\,x^{\pi}\right]\right\}\ . (3.1)

This value is fixed once the action is selected and random across samples and policy randomization.

Comparison and decomposition.

The following comparison and resulting identity isolate the two components of combined-risk regret. Let X:=c⁡(xπ,ξ)X:=c(x^{\pi},\xi), and let t∗t^{\ast} attain the variational representation of CVaRδ​[X]\text{CVaR}_{\delta}[X] in equation (2.2). For every realized (ξ1n,xπ)(\xi_{1}^{n},x^{\pi}),

Ψnπ≤t∗+11−δ𝔼[(X−t∗)+|ξ1n,xπ],\Psi_{n}^{\pi}\penalty\ \leq\penalty\ t^{\ast}+\frac{1}{1-\delta}\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[(X-t^{\ast})^{+}\,\middle|\,\xi_{1}^{n},x^{\pi}\right],

because the conditional variational formula defining Ψnπ\Psi_{n}^{\pi} minimizes over all thresholds, and t∗t^{\ast} is one feasible threshold. Taking expectations over (ξ1n,xπ)(\xi_{1}^{n},x^{\pi}) yields

𝔼ξ1n,xπ​[Ψnπ]≤CVaRδ​[c⁡(xπ,ξ)].\mathbb{E}_{\xi_{1}^{n},\,x^{\pi}}\!\left[\Psi_{n}^{\pi}\right]\penalty\ \leq\penalty\ \text{CVaR}_{\delta}[c\left(x^{\pi},\xi\right)]. (3.2)

Adding and subtracting 𝔼ξ1n,xπ​[Ψnπ]\mathbb{E}_{\xi_{1}^{n},\,x^{\pi}}[\Psi_{n}^{\pi}] in (2.7) gives

ℛδ,n​(π,F)=(𝔼ξ1n,xπ​[Ψnπ]−OPTδ​(F))⏟PSδ,n​(π,F)– expected post-sample regret+(CVaRδ​[c⁡(xπ,ξ)]−𝔼ξ1n,xπ​[Ψnπ])⏟SRδ,n​(π,F)​– sample-risk premium.\mathcal{R}_{\delta,n}\left(\pi,F\right)=\underbrace{\Bigl(\mathbb{E}_{\xi_{1}^{n},\,x^{\pi}}\!\left[\Psi_{n}^{\pi}\right]-\text{OPT}_{\delta}\left(F\right)\Bigr)}_{\text{$\mathrm{PS}_{\delta,n}(\pi,F)$-- expected post-sample regret}}+\underbrace{\Bigl(\text{CVaR}_{\delta}[c\left(x^{\pi},\xi\right)]-\mathbb{E}_{\xi_{1}^{n},\,x^{\pi}}\!\left[\Psi_{n}^{\pi}\right]\Bigr)}_{\mathrm{SR}_{\delta,n}(\pi,F)\text{-- sample-risk premium}}. (3.3)

Both brackets are nonnegative. For every realized (ξ1n,xπ)(\xi_{1}^{n},x^{\pi}) the induced action is a feasible deterministic action, so Ψnπ≥OPTδ​(F)\Psi_{n}^{\pi}\geq\text{OPT}_{\delta}(F), and taking expectations establishes nonnegativity of the first. We call it the expected post-sample regret PSδ,n​(π,F)\mathrm{PS}_{\delta,n}\!\left(\pi,F\right): the expected outcome-only tail-risk gap of the selected action relative to the oracle, averaged over samples and policy randomization. The second bracket is nonnegative by equation (3.2), and it measures something the first cannot see. Combined-risk CVaR evaluates the induced loss over the sample, the policy randomization, and the future outcome together. Its excess over the average outcome-only CVaR can be positive even when every selected action is optimal, as Example 3.1 below shows. Under expected cost this excess vanishes by the tower property. We call this additional severity the sample-risk premium SRδ,n​(π,F)\mathrm{SR}_{\delta,n}\!\left(\pi,F\right). For independent deployments under the same FF, π\pi, and nn, the average of the outcome-only values Ψnπ\Psi_{n}^{\pi} converges to 𝔼⁡[Ψnπ]\mathbb{E}[\Psi_{n}^{\pi}]. The gap between this limit and the combined-risk CVaR is SRδ,n​(π,F)\mathrm{SR}_{\delta,n}\!\left(\pi,F\right).

The premium as the price of one shared cutoff.

The premium admits a form that makes this additional severity explicit. Because the induced action xπx^{\pi} is independent of the future outcome ξ∼F\xi\sim F, both terms in the premium can be expressed through the fixed-action variational objective ϕF​(x,t)\phi_{F}\!\left(x,t\right) from equation (2.3). Combined-risk CVaR in equation (2.5) optimizes over a single threshold that has to serve every realized action at once, so that it equals inft𝔼xπ​[ϕF​(xπ,t)]\inf_{t}\mathbb{E}_{x^{\pi}}[\phi_{F}\!\left(x^{\pi},t\right)]. The post-sample evaluation minimizes the threshold separately for each realized action, giving Ψnπ=inftϕF​(xπ,t)=QF​(xπ)\Psi_{n}^{\pi}=\inf_{t}\phi_{F}\!\left(x^{\pi},t\right)=Q_{F}\!\left(x^{\pi}\right). Subtracting the second from the first,

SRδ,n​(π,F)=inft∈ℝ𝔼xπ​[ϕF​(xπ,t)]−𝔼xπ​[inft∈ℝϕF​(xπ,t)]=inft∈ℝ𝔼xπ​[ϕF​(xπ,t)]−𝔼xπ​[QF​(xπ)]\mathrm{SR}_{\delta,n}\!\left(\pi,F\right)\penalty\ =\penalty\ \inf_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{E}_{x^{\pi}}\!\left[\phi_{F}\!\left(x^{\pi},t\right)\right]\penalty\ -\penalty\ \mathbb{E}_{x^{\pi}}\!\left[\inf_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\phi_{F}\!\left(x^{\pi},t\right)\right]\penalty\ =\penalty\ \inf_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{E}_{x^{\pi}}\!\left[\phi_{F}\!\left(x^{\pi},t\right)\right]\penalty\ -\penalty\ \mathbb{E}_{x^{\pi}}\!\left[Q_{F}\!\left(x^{\pi}\right)\right] (3.4)

The premium is the cost of using a single threshold across the induced loss distributions: it is the gap between the infimum of an expectation and the expectation of the pointwise infimum. The threshold is an auxiliary variable in the CVaR representation. Example 3.1 makes that gap strict. Both actions are optimal for outcome-only CVaR, with minimizing cutoffs 11 and 00, so the difference in (3.4) is positive and the combined-risk regret equals the premium.

Example 3.1 (Premium without a bad action).

Fix δ=1/2\delta=1/2, let 𝒳={0,1}\mathcal{X}=\{0,1\}, and let ξ\xi equal 00 or 22 with probabilities 3/43/4 and 1/41/4. Set c⁡(0,ξ)=1c(0,\xi)=1 and c⁡(1,ξ)=ξc(1,\xi)=\xi. Both actions have outcome-only CVaR equal to 11, with cutoffs 11 and 00. For any n≥1n\geq 1, consider the deterministic policy that selects action 00 if the first training observation is 22 and action 11 otherwise. Against an independent future outcome, its losses 00, 11, and 22 have probabilities 9/169/16, 4/164/16, and 3/163/16. Its combined-risk CVaR is therefore 5/45/4: expected post-sample regret is zero, while the sample-risk premium is 1/41/4.

The next proposition characterizes when a common threshold minimizes the objective for almost every induced action.

When each component vanishes.

The following proposition characterizes when each component vanishes. Before we state it, we write

𝒯δ​(x):=arg⁡mint​ϕF​(x,t)\mathcal{T}_{\delta}(x)\penalty\ \penalty\ :=\penalty\ \penalty\ \arg\min_{t}\phi_{F}\!\left(x,t\right)

for the set of minimizing thresholds at the action xx. The conditional tails induced by xπx^{\pi} are aligned if one threshold lies in 𝒯δ​(xπ)\mathcal{T}_{\delta}(x^{\pi}) for almost every realized action, and misaligned otherwise.

Proposition 3.2 (Endpoints of the two components).

Suppose that xπx^{\pi} is independent of ξ∼F\xi\sim F and that

𝔼xπ,ξ​|c⁡(xπ,ξ)|<∞.\mathbb{E}_{x^{\pi},\xi}|c(x^{\pi},\xi)|<\infty\ .

Then the following hold.

  1. 1.

    SRδ,n​(π,F)=0\mathrm{SR}_{\delta,n}\!\left(\pi,F\right)=0 if and only if the conditional tails induced by xπx^{\pi} are aligned. In particular, the premium vanishes whenever xπx^{\pi} is degenerate.

  2. 2.

    Suppose in addition that the infimum defining OPTδ​(F)\text{OPT}_{\delta}(F) is attained, and let 𝒳F∗:=arg⁡minx∈𝒳​QF​(x)\mathcal{X}^{*}_{F}:=\arg\min_{x\in\mathcal{X}}Q_{F}\!\left(x\right) denote the set of oracle actions. Then PSδ,n​(π,F)=0\mathrm{PS}_{\delta,n}\!\left(\pi,F\right)=0 if and only if xπ∈𝒳F∗x^{\pi}\in\mathcal{X}^{*}_{F} almost surely. If the oracle action is unique, this holds if and only if xπ=xF∗x^{\pi}=x^{*}_{F} almost surely.

In words: PS\mathrm{PS} vanishes if and only if the policy plays an oracle action almost surely; SR\mathrm{SR} vanishes if and only if the induced loss distributions admit a common minimizing threshold, and a degenerate action is always aligned. Distinct selected VaR values can still yield zero premium when their sets of minimizing thresholds overlap. The proof is in Appendix A.1. A complementary bound controls the premium at every sample size through the distribution of the induced cutoff.

Proposition 3.3 (An upper bound on the sample-risk premium).

Under the independence and integrability hypotheses of Proposition 3.2, let Y=qF​(xπ)Y=q_{F}(x^{\pi}) and Lδ=max⁡{1,δ/(1−δ)}L_{\delta}=\max\{1,\delta/(1-\delta)\}. Then YY is integrable and

0≤SRδ,n​(π,F)≤CVaRδ​[Y]−𝔼​Y≤Lδ​inft∈ℝ𝔼​|Y−t|.0\leq\mathrm{SR}_{\delta,n}\!\left(\pi,F\right)\leq\text{CVaR}_{\delta}[Y]-\mathbb{E}Y\leq L_{\delta}\inf_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{E}|Y-t|. (3.5)

The proof is in Appendix A.2. Equality holds between the premium and CVaRδ​[Y]−𝔼​Y\text{CVaR}_{\delta}[Y]-\mathbb{E}Y when the loss is conditionally deterministic. That middle term keeps the asymmetric tail weighting that the absolute-deviation bound discards. Corollary A.1 records the rate that follows from the bound: under the Lipschitz condition (2.6), if xπ=x∗+rn​Znx^{\pi}=x^{*}+r_{n}Z_{n}, rn→0r_{n}\to 0, supn𝔼​|Zn|<∞\sup_{n}\mathbb{E}|Z_{n}|<\infty, and qFq_{F} is differentiable at x∗x^{*}, then SR=O⁡(rn)\mathrm{SR}=O(r_{n}). Its proof is in Appendix A.3. The atomic regime below attains this upper order. The rate conclusion uses the cutoff and moment conditions; other orders remain possible outside the regimes below.

We first establish the orders of the two components for policies concentrating on a unique oracle action. We then quantify their leading coefficients in the smooth and atomic regimes, and examine when a component remains positive in the limit.

3.1 The asymptotic order of the components

The curvature of the outcome-only objective determines the local cost of action error. The movement of the cutoff and the behavior of the loss distribution around it determine the premium. The following results translate a policy concentration rate rnr_{n} into orders of regret under the stated moment and regularity conditions. Section 4 establishes such concentration for SAA under additional hypotheses.

Theorem 3.4 (Smooth regime).

Under Assumption 2.2, suppose that equation (2.6) holds. Fix FF and δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), and let x∗x^{*} be the unique oracle action. Suppose x∗x^{*} is interior and that QFQ_{F} is twice differentiable at x∗x^{*} with 0<QF′′​(x∗)<∞0<Q_{F}^{\prime\prime}(x^{*})<\infty. Write q∗:=qF​(x∗)q^{*}:=q_{F}\!\left(x^{*}\right). Suppose c⁡(x,ξ)c(x,\xi) has a density gx​(t)g_{x}(t) for (x,t)(x,t) near (x∗,q∗)(x^{*},q^{*}), that the map (x,t)↦gx​(t)(x,t)\mapsto g_{x}(t) is continuous at (x∗,q∗)(x^{*},q^{*}), and that 0<gx∗​(q∗)<∞0<g_{x^{*}}(q^{*})<\infty. Suppose the policy concentrates on x∗x^{*} at rate rnr_{n},

xπ=x∗+rn​Zn,rn↘0,Zn⇒Z,x^{\pi}\penalty\ \penalty\ =\penalty\ \penalty\ x^{*}+r_{n}Z_{n}\ ,\qquad r_{n}\searrow 0\ ,\qquad Z_{n}\Rightarrow Z\ , (3.6)

and that qF′​(x∗)≠0q_{F}^{\prime}(x^{*})\neq 0, so the cutoff moves to first order with the action. Suppose {|Zn|2}\bigl\{|Z_{n}|^{2}\bigr\} is uniformly integrable and ZZ is nondegenerate. Then

PSδ,n​(π,F)=Θ⁡(rn2),SRδ,n​(π,F)=Θ⁡(rn2).\mathrm{PS}_{\delta,n}\!\left(\pi,F\right)\penalty\ \penalty\ =\penalty\ \penalty\ \Theta\!\left(r_{n}^{2}\right)\ ,\qquad\mathrm{SR}_{\delta,n}\!\left(\pi,F\right)\penalty\ \penalty\ =\penalty\ \penalty\ \Theta\!\left(r_{n}^{2}\right)\ .

The proof is in Appendix A.4. Theorem 3.4 characterizes the regime in which the policy concentrates around a unique oracle action. The relative order of the two regret components is determined by three features: the local growth of the outcome-only CVaR objective away from the oracle action, the order at which the VaR\mathrm{VaR} moves with the action, and the local growth of the variational objective around the VaR\mathrm{VaR}. When the outcome-only CVaR objective is locally quadratic, the variational objective is locally quadratic around the VaR\mathrm{VaR}, and the VaR\mathrm{VaR} moves to first order with the action, the two regret components are of the same order.

A squared loss against a skewed outcome illustrates the smooth regime when the loss density satisfies the theorem’s conditions, the cutoff slope is nonzero, and the oracle is unique and interior with positive finite curvature. Table 1 evaluates the local coefficient for this loss. Symmetry can instead make qF′​(x∗)=0q_{F}^{\prime}(x^{*})=0, outside the theorem’s scope. Proposition 3.6 identifies the limiting ratio under these same hypotheses. For centered limiting fluctuations, the coefficient can be thousands even though the two components have the same order.

Under the moving-atom, straddling, and isolation conditions below, the premium is linear in the concentration scale, while post-sample regret remains quadratic.

Theorem 3.5 (Atomic regime).

Under Assumption 2.2, suppose that equation (2.6) holds. Let x∗x^{*} be the unique interior oracle action, and suppose QFQ_{F} is twice differentiable there with 0<QF′′​(x∗)<∞0<Q_{F}^{\prime\prime}(x^{*})<\infty. Suppose the loss places an atom at a level ℓ⁡(x)\ell(x), continuously differentiable near x∗x^{*}, with ℓ⁡(x∗)=q∗:=qF​(x∗)\ell(x^{*})=q^{*}:=q_{F}\!\left(x^{*}\right) and ℓ′​(x∗)≠0\ell^{\prime}(x^{*})\neq 0, and that the atom strictly straddles the tail level,

ℙ⁡(c⁡(x∗,ξ)<q∗)<δ<ℙ⁡(c⁡(x∗,ξ)≤q∗).\mathbb{P}\bigl(c(x^{*},\xi)<q^{*}\bigr)\penalty\ <\penalty\ \delta\penalty\ <\penalty\ \mathbb{P}\bigl(c(x^{*},\xi)\leq q^{*}\bigr)\ .

As the action approaches the oracle and the margin around ℓ⁡(x)\ell(x) shrinks, the probability strictly above the atom and the probability at or above a level just below it settle at their oracle values,

lim(x,u)→(x∗,0+)ℙ⁡(c⁡(x,ξ)>ℓ⁡(x)+u)\displaystyle\lim_{\left(x,u\right)\to\left(x^{*},0^{+}\right)}\mathbb{P}\bigl(c\left(x,\xi\right)>\ell\left(x\right)+u\bigr)\penalty =ℙ⁡(c⁡(x∗,ξ)>q∗),\displaystyle=\penalty\ \mathbb{P}\bigl(c\left(x^{*},\xi\right)>q^{*}\bigr)\ , (3.7)
lim(x,u)→(x∗,0+)ℙ⁡(c⁡(x,ξ)≥ℓ⁡(x)−u)\displaystyle\lim_{\left(x,u\right)\to\left(x^{*},0^{+}\right)}\mathbb{P}\bigl(c\left(x,\xi\right)\geq\ell\left(x\right)-u\bigr)\penalty =ℙ⁡(c⁡(x∗,ξ)≥q∗).\displaystyle=\penalty\ \mathbb{P}\bigl(c\left(x^{*},\xi\right)\geq q^{*}\bigr)\ .

These limits are the isolation assumption. Other losses may approach the atom; only the probability in a shrinking band is controlled. Suppose that the policy concentrates on x∗x^{*} as in equation (3.6), with {|Zn|2}\bigl\{|Z_{n}|^{2}\bigr\} uniformly integrable and ZZ nondegenerate. Then

PSδ,n​(π,F)=Θ⁡(rn2),SRδ,n​(π,F)=Θ⁡(rn).\mathrm{PS}_{\delta,n}\!\left(\pi,F\right)\penalty\ \penalty\ =\penalty\ \penalty\ \Theta\!\left(r_{n}^{2}\right)\ ,\qquad\mathrm{SR}_{\delta,n}\!\left(\pi,F\right)\penalty\ \penalty\ =\penalty\ \penalty\ \Theta\!\left(r_{n}\right)\ .

The proof is in Appendix A.14. The profit formulation of the newsvendor illustrates an atom created by the loss: when demand meets or exceeds the order, the loss is constant at a level that moves with the order. At the oracle, this atom strictly straddles the tail level; continuous demand gives the isolation condition (Besbes and Rieger 2026). With a unique interior oracle, a demand distribution differentiable there with a positive finite derivative, and a policy satisfying the theorem’s concentration and moment conditions, the problem lies in the atomic regime. Multiple optimal orders can instead produce the mixing behavior discussed below. More generally, an atom yields the stated orders only under the full hypotheses of Theorem 3.5. Under these hypotheses, the sample-risk premium is the leading component of combined-risk regret: its ratio to expected post-sample regret diverges.

3.2 Mean squared error plus a KK-weighted variance penalty

In the smooth regime, the common rate of decay does not determine the relative magnitude of the two components. The next proposition shows that PS\mathrm{PS} is asymptotically proportional to the mean squared error of the action about x∗x^{*}, while SR\mathrm{SR} is asymptotically proportional to its variance, and identifies the two constants.

Proposition 3.6 (Smooth-regime coefficients).

Suppose that the hypotheses of Theorem 3.4 hold. Write q∗:=qF​(x∗)q^{*}:=q_{F}\!\left(x^{*}\right), g:=gx∗​(q∗)g:=g_{x^{*}}(q^{*}), MSE:=𝔼⁡[(xπ−x∗)2]\mathrm{MSE}:=\mathbb{E}[(x^{\pi}-x^{*})^{2}], and V:=Var​(xπ)V:=\text{Var}(x^{\pi}). Then

PSδ,n​(π,F)MSE⟶12​QF′′​(x∗),SRδ,n​(π,F)V⟶g⋅qF′​(x∗)22​(1−δ).\frac{\mathrm{PS}_{\delta,n}\!\left(\pi,F\right)}{\mathrm{MSE}}\penalty\ \penalty\ \longrightarrow\penalty\ \penalty\ \frac{1}{2}Q_{F}^{\prime\prime}\!\left(x^{*}\right)\ ,\qquad\frac{\mathrm{SR}_{\delta,n}\!\left(\pi,F\right)}{V}\penalty\ \penalty\ \longrightarrow\penalty\ \penalty\ \frac{g\cdot q_{F}^{\prime}\!\left(x^{*}\right)^{2}}{2\left(1-\delta\right)}\ . (3.8)

The proof is in Appendix A.8. The ratio of the two constants is the relative variance penalty,

K=g⋅qF′​(x∗)2(1−δ)​QF′′​(x∗).\boxed{\;K\;=\;\dfrac{g\cdot q_{F}^{\prime}\!\left(x^{*}\right)^{2}}{\left(1-\delta\right)\,Q_{F}^{\prime\prime}\!\left(x^{*}\right)}\;}\ . (3.9)

Together, these limits give the local expansion

PSδ,n​(π,F)+SRδ,n​(π,F)=12​QF′′​(x∗)​[MSE+K⋅V]+o⁡(rn2).\mathrm{PS}_{\delta,n}\!\left(\pi,F\right)+\mathrm{SR}_{\delta,n}\!\left(\pi,F\right)\penalty\ \penalty\ =\penalty\ \penalty\ \tfrac{1}{2}Q_{F}^{\prime\prime}\!\left(x^{*}\right)\bigl[\mathrm{MSE}+K\cdot V\bigr]+o\!\left(r_{n}^{2}\right)\ . (3.10)

Since MSE=(𝔼⁡[xπ−x∗])2+V\mathrm{MSE}=\bigl(\mathbb{E}[x^{\pi}-x^{*}]\bigr)^{2}+V, variance receives weight 1+K1+K relative to squared bias in the leading term.

Why the premium can be large.

The coefficient compares two local curvatures. Let AFA_{F} be the action curvature when the threshold is held at q∗=qF​(x∗)q^{*}=q_{F}(x^{*}). The smooth local expansion gives

ϕF​(x∗+h,q∗)=QF​(x∗)+12​AF​h2+o⁡(h2),AF=QF′′​(x∗)+g​qF′​(x∗)21−δ.\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \phi_{F}(x^{*}+h,q^{*})&=Q_{F}(x^{*})+\tfrac{1}{2}A_{F}h^{2}+o(h^{2}),\\ A_{F}&=Q_{F}^{\prime\prime}(x^{*})+\frac{g\,q_{F}^{\prime}(x^{*})^{2}}{1-\delta}.\end{aligned} (3.11)

Thus 1+K=AF/QF′′​(x∗)1+K=A_{F}/Q_{F}^{\prime\prime}(x^{*}). Post-sample evaluation allows a separate minimizing threshold for each selected action. Combined evaluation uses one threshold across samples; locally, it adjusts to the mean action but not to each fluctuation. In the leading regret term, squared bias is therefore charged at curvature QF′′​(x∗)Q_{F}^{\prime\prime}(x^{*}) and variance at AFA_{F}. The additional variance curvature in the premium is AF−QF′′​(x∗)A_{F}-Q_{F}^{\prime\prime}(x^{*}). For the squared loss with lognormal outcomes in Table 1 at δ=0.99\delta=0.99, the optimized and fixed-threshold curvatures are approximately 1.851.85 and 72347234. Appendix A.10 derives the expansion under the existing smooth-regime hypotheses.

To express the relative magnitude of the two components, write

ρn:=SRδ,n​(π,F)PSδ,n​(π,F)\rho_{n}\penalty\ \penalty\ :=\penalty\ \penalty\ \frac{\mathrm{SR}_{\delta,n}\!\left(\pi,F\right)}{\mathrm{PS}_{\delta,n}\!\left(\pi,F\right)} (3.12)

whenever PSδ,n​(π,F)>0\mathrm{PS}_{\delta,n}\!\left(\pi,F\right)>0. Combined regret is then (1+ρn)(1+\rho_{n}) times PSδ,n​(π,F)\mathrm{PS}_{\delta,n}\!\left(\pi,F\right). Under the smooth-regime hypotheses, the ratio converges to a positive finite constant whose magnitude can be large.

Corollary 3.7 (The limiting premium ratio in the smooth regime).

Under the hypotheses of Proposition 3.6, suppose in addition that 𝔼⁡[Z]=0\mathbb{E}[Z]=0. Then

ρn⟶K,\rho_{n}\penalty\ \penalty\ \longrightarrow\penalty\ \penalty\ K\ , (3.13)

with KK the relative variance penalty in equation (3.9). Without the centering assumption the limit is K⋅Var​(Z)/𝔼⁡[Z2]K\cdot\text{Var}(Z)/\mathbb{E}[Z^{2}].

The proof is in Appendix A.9. A nonzero mean of the limiting scaled error ZZ lowers the limiting ratio by the factor Var​(Z)/𝔼​[Z2]\text{Var}(Z)/\mathbb{E}[Z^{2}]. For fixed (c,F,δ)(c,F,\delta), KK is the largest limiting ratio under Proposition 3.6, attained when 𝔼⁡[Z]=0\mathbb{E}[Z]=0. Table 1 evaluates KK for squared loss using the formula in Proposition A.6. In the tabulated examples, KK increases over the reported tail levels. It reaches the tens of thousands for the lognormal family, while lying below one for the gamma family at lower tail levels.

For centered limiting fluctuations, the premium’s share of combined-risk regret converges to K/(1+K)K/(1+K). Thus the lognormal entry K≈3900K\approx 3900 at δ=0.99\delta=0.99 corresponds to a limiting share of approximately 99.97%99.97\%. The coefficient KK describes a local limit; the results do not specify the sample size at which ρn\rho_{n} is close to it. Finite-sample accuracy depends on both the spread of the learned action and the neighborhood over which the density and cutoff expansions are accurate.

The zero-slope endpoint is different. If the other hypotheses of Theorem 3.4 hold but qF′​(x∗)=0q_{F}^{\prime}(x^{*})=0, then SR=o⁡(rn2)\mathrm{SR}=o(r_{n}^{2}) while PS=Θ⁡(rn2)\mathrm{PS}=\Theta(r_{n}^{2}). Proposition A.5 records these orders. Its proof evaluates the common threshold at q∗q^{*}. Thus action variability need not create a premium of the same order as post-sample regret.

3.3 When the cutoff sits on an atom

The reduction in equation (3.10) prices a smooth cutoff by mean squared error and a variance. Under the hypotheses of Theorem 3.5, the unique minimizing threshold near x∗x^{*} is the atom level, qF​(x)=ℓ​(x)q_{F}(x)=\ell(x). Hence qF′​(x∗)=ℓ′​(x∗)≠0q_{F}^{\prime}(x^{*})=\ell^{\prime}(x^{*})\neq 0, and the variational objective grows linearly away from this threshold. The leading premium is then a weighted absolute deviation of the induced cutoff. This dispersion is invariant under deterministic translations of the scaled cutoff fluctuations, while the leading post-sample term continues to charge mean squared error. Write p:=ℙ⁡(c⁡(x∗,ξ)=q∗)p:=\mathbb{P}(c(x^{*},\xi)=q^{*}) for the mass at the cutoff, and

τ:=δ−ℙ⁡(c⁡(x∗,ξ)<q∗)p\tau\penalty\ :=\penalty\ \frac{\delta-\mathbb{P}\bigl(c(x^{*},\xi)<q^{*}\bigr)}{p} (3.14)

for the fraction of that mass lying below δ\delta. The fraction above δ\delta is 1−τ1-\tau. For any integrable random variable YY, define 𝒲⁡(Y):=p​inft∈ℝ𝔼⁡[τ​(Y−t)++(1−τ)​(t−Y)+]\mathcal{W}(Y):=p\inf_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{E}[\tau(Y-t)^{+}+(1-\tau)(t-Y)^{+}]. A τ\tau-quantile attains the infimum. Letting qτq_{\tau} be such a quantile of the induced VaR\mathrm{VaR}, this gives

𝒲⁡(qF​(xπ))=p​𝔼​[τ​(qF​(xπ)−qτ)++(1−τ)​(qτ−qF​(xπ))+].\mathcal{W}\!\left(q_{F}\!\left(x^{\pi}\right)\right)\penalty\ \penalty\ =\penalty\ \penalty\ p\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\tau\bigl(q_{F}\!\left(x^{\pi}\right)-q_{\tau}\bigr)^{+}+(1-\tau)\bigl(q_{\tau}-q_{F}\!\left(x^{\pi}\right)\bigr)^{+}\right]\ . (3.15)
Proposition 3.8 (Atom at the cutoff).

Suppose that the hypotheses of Theorem 3.5 hold, and write MSE\mathrm{MSE} as in Proposition 3.6. Then

PSδ,n​(π,F)MSE⟶12​QF′′​(x∗),SRδ,n​(π,F)𝒲⁡(qF​(xπ))⟶11−δ.\frac{\mathrm{PS}_{\delta,n}\!\left(\pi,F\right)}{\mathrm{MSE}}\penalty\ \penalty\ \longrightarrow\penalty\ \penalty\ \tfrac{1}{2}Q_{F}^{\prime\prime}\!\left(x^{*}\right)\ ,\qquad\frac{\mathrm{SR}_{\delta,n}\!\left(\pi,F\right)}{\mathcal{W}\!\left(q_{F}\!\left(x^{\pi}\right)\right)}\penalty\ \penalty\ \longrightarrow\penalty\ \penalty\ \frac{1}{1-\delta}\ . (3.16)

The proof is in Appendix A.16. The induced VaR\mathrm{VaR} moves with the action because qF′​(x∗)≠0q_{F}^{\prime}(x^{*})\neq 0. When the two gaps in the straddling hypothesis are equal, τ=1/2\tau=1/2 and 𝒲⁡(qF​(xπ))\mathcal{W}\!\left(q_{F}\!\left(x^{\pi}\right)\right) is (p/2)(p/2) times the mean absolute deviation of the induced VaR\mathrm{VaR} about a median. The two limits have different remainders, so they are recorded separately,

PSδ,n​(π,F)=12​QF′′​(x∗)​MSE+o⁡(rn2),SRδ,n​(π,F)=𝒲⁡(qF​(xπ))1−δ+o⁡(rn).\mathrm{PS}_{\delta,n}\!\left(\pi,F\right)\penalty\ \penalty\ =\penalty\ \penalty\ \tfrac{1}{2}Q_{F}^{\prime\prime}\!\left(x^{*}\right)\,\mathrm{MSE}+o(r_{n}^{2})\ ,\qquad\mathrm{SR}_{\delta,n}\!\left(\pi,F\right)\penalty\ \penalty\ =\penalty\ \penalty\ \frac{\mathcal{W}\!\left(q_{F}\!\left(x^{\pi}\right)\right)}{1-\delta}+o(r_{n})\ . (3.17)

The error in the premium is of order o⁡(rn)o(r_{n}). That remainder can exceed the quadratic post-sample term, so the sum is an expansion of total regret up to o⁡(rn)o(r_{n}). At small action spreads the linear premium dominates the quadratic post-sample term, the same comparison the atomic regime records asymptotically.

The cutoff expansion holds in first mean: qF​(xπ)−q∗=qF′​(x∗)​rn​Zn+oL1​(rn)q_{F}\!\left(x^{\pi}\right)-q^{*}=q_{F}^{\prime}(x^{*})\,r_{n}Z_{n}+o_{L^{1}}(r_{n}). Weak convergence and uniform integrability give convergence of the scaled cutoff distributions in the Wasserstein-11 metric. The weighted deviation is continuous in this metric, positively homogeneous, and invariant under deterministic translations. Applying it with the same level τ\tau to qF′​(x∗)​Zq_{F}^{\prime}(x^{*})Z yields

rn​ρn⟶2​𝒲​(qF′​(x∗)​Z)(1−δ)​QF′′​(x∗)​𝔼​[Z2].r_{n}\,\rho_{n}\penalty\ \penalty\ \longrightarrow\penalty\ \penalty\ \frac{2\,\mathcal{W}\!\left(q_{F}^{\prime}(x^{*})\,Z\right)}{(1-\delta)\,Q_{F}^{\prime\prime}\!\left(x^{*}\right)\,\mathbb{E}[Z^{2}]}\ . (3.18)

The weights are a property of (c,F,δ)(c,F,\delta) at the oracle action and carry no sample size. The numerator of ρn\rho_{n} is homogeneous of degree one and the denominator of degree two, so at a concentration rate rnr_{n} the ratio is of order 1/rn1/r_{n}, and equation (3.18) names the constant. The premium therefore outgrows PSδ,n​(π,F)\mathrm{PS}_{\delta,n}\!\left(\pi,F\right) in order and not merely in constant, which is what Theorem 3.5 records. For the newsvendor loss under the conditions of Theorem 3.5, the ratio of the premium to expected post-sample regret grows like 1/rn1/r_{n}. Besbes and Rieger (2026) specialize Proposition 3.8 to that loss: they record the limit of PS\mathrm{PS} over mean squared error and the limit of the premium over a weighted absolute deviation of the order.

3.4 Regimes in which a component does not vanish

Uniqueness of xF∗x^{*}_{F}, which Theorems 3.4 and 3.5 both assume, excludes a qualitatively different regime. When several actions attain the oracle value, a data-driven policy may converge to the set of optimal actions without converging to any single one of them. In that case, the expected post-sample regret may vanish even though the induced action remains nondegenerate. If no threshold minimizes the variational objective for almost every limiting action, the sample-risk premium can converge to a strictly positive constant. The following proposition formalizes this possibility.

Proposition 3.9.

Suppose that the unconditional action distribution, over the sample and any policy randomization, satisfies xπ⇒x∞πx^{\pi}\Rightarrow x_{\infty}^{\pi}, where x∞πx_{\infty}^{\pi} is supported on the set of population-optimal actions. Suppose further that x↦c⁡(x,ξ)x\mapsto c(x,\xi) is continuous at x∞πx_{\infty}^{\pi} almost surely, and that the family

{|c⁡(xπ,ξ)|}n≥1\left\{|c(x^{\pi},\xi)|\right\}_{n\geq 1}

is uniformly integrable. Then

PSδ,n​(π,F)⟶0.\mathrm{PS}_{\delta,n}(\pi,F)\longrightarrow 0.

Moreover, if

ℙ⁡(t∈𝒯δ​(x∞π))<1for every ​t∈ℝ,\mathbb{P}\!\left(t\in\mathcal{T}_{\delta}(x_{\infty}^{\pi})\right)<1\qquad\text{for every }t\in\mathbb{R}\ ,

then

SRδ,n​(π,F)⟶SRδ,∞​(π,F)>0.\mathrm{SR}_{\delta,n}(\pi,F)\longrightarrow\mathrm{SR}_{\delta,\infty}(\pi,F)>0.

Consequently,

PSδ,n​(π,F)=o⁡(1),SRδ,n​(π,F)=Θ⁡(1).\mathrm{PS}_{\delta,n}(\pi,F)=o(1),\qquad\mathrm{SR}_{\delta,n}(\pi,F)=\Theta(1).

The proof is in Appendix A.17. The cost and FF determine the optimal actions and their sets of minimizing thresholds. The policy determines whether its limiting action remains nondegenerate on that optimal set. Under the proposition’s hypotheses, this limiting mixture has vanishing post-sample regret and a positive premium precisely when it has no common minimizing threshold. A policy converging to a single optimal action has vanishing premium. For example, in the newsvendor problem, SAA at a particular Bernoulli distribution keeps mixing optimal orders with no common minimizing threshold, and its premium tends to a positive constant. A window of order-statistic indices wider than the n\sqrt{n} fluctuations of the binomial count concentrates on one limiting optimal order and eliminates that persistent premium (Besbes and Rieger 2026).

The displaced regime keeps a unique oracle action and allows persistent displacement from it.

Proposition 3.10.

Fix FF and suppose that the population problem has a unique optimal action xF∗x_{F}^{*} satisfying

κF(ε):=infx∈𝒳:|x−xF∗|≥ε{CVaRδ,ξ∼F[c(x,ξ)]−OPTδ(F)}>0\kappa_{F}(\varepsilon):=\inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\in\mathcal{X}:\\ |x-x_{F}^{*}|\geq\varepsilon\end{subarray}}\left\{\text{CVaR}_{\delta,\xi\sim F}[c(x,\xi)]-\text{OPT}_{\delta}(F)\right\}>0

for every ε>0\varepsilon>0. If, for some ε>0\varepsilon>0 and η>0\eta>0,

lim infn→∞ℙF​(|xπ−xF∗|≥ε)≥η,\displaystyle\liminf_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}_{F}\!\left(|x^{\pi}-x_{F}^{*}|\geq\varepsilon\right)\geq\eta,

then

lim infn→∞PSδ,n​(π,F)≥η​κF​(ε)>0,\displaystyle\liminf_{n\to\infty}\mathrm{PS}_{\delta,n}(\pi,F)\geq\eta\,\kappa_{F}(\varepsilon)>0,

and hence

PSδ,n​(π,F)=Ω⁡(1).\displaystyle\mathrm{PS}_{\delta,n}(\pi,F)=\Omega(1).

We prove the proposition in Appendix A.19. The same bound yields the form used below: if xF∗x_{F}^{*} is well separated and PSδ,n​(π,F)→0\mathrm{PS}_{\delta,n}(\pi,F)\to 0, then xπ→xF∗x^{\pi}\to x_{F}^{*} in probability.

A policy enters this regime when it remains away from the oracle with probability bounded below. This occurs, for example, if it converges to a surrogate-objective optimum different from xF∗x_{F}^{*}, or to the best action in a restricted family whose optimum differs from xF∗x_{F}^{*}. Shrinking an otherwise consistent action toward a distinct fixed anchor with a weight converging to a positive constant also gives a displaced limit. Confining the policy to actions outside a neighborhood of xF∗x_{F}^{*}, while the oracle continues to minimize over 𝒳\mathcal{X}, forces persistent displacement directly. These mechanisms satisfy the proposition when the oracle is well separated.

3.5 A summary of the regimes

Theorems 3.4 and 3.5, Proposition 3.9 and Proposition 3.10 provide a spectrum of possibilities for the relative importance of the two regret components. The spectrum covers a wide variety of cost functions and distributions. However, it is not a partition: other combinations of the policy, the cost, and FF are possible, and the decomposition is not characterized for every one of them. These regimes are summarized in Table 2.

Under the stated hypotheses of the smooth and atomic regimes, the sample-risk premium is of at least the same order as expected post-sample regret. Equal orders do not imply similar magnitudes. For centered limiting fluctuations in the smooth regime, the premium ratio tends to KK, which reaches thousands in Table 1. The atomic regime attains the O⁡(rn)O(r_{n}) upper order from Proposition 3.3 under the stated cutoff and moment conditions. Other orders remain possible outside the representative regimes. Section 4 shows that sample average approximation is consistent at a unique well-separated oracle under a compact action set and a loss that is continuous in the action and uniformly bounded. The displaced regime is then avoided. In the atomic regime the sample-risk premium is of larger order than the expected post-sample regret.

4 Regret of SAA

We now establish the concentration properties of sample average approximation (SAA) needed to apply Section 3, and use them to determine the rates of its two regret components. Throughout this section, FF and δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1) are fixed.

Sample average approximation replaces FF by the empirical distribution F^n\hat{F}_{n} and minimizes the resulting CVaR. For ξ∼F^n\xi\sim\hat{F}_{n},

CVaRδ,ξ∼F^n[c(x,ξ)]=inft{t+11−δ⋅1n∑i=1n(c(x,ξi)−t)+}\text{CVaR}_{\delta,\xi\sim\hat{F}_{n}}\left[c\left(x,\xi\right)\right]\penalty\ \penalty\ =\penalty\ \penalty\ \inf_{t}\left\{t+\frac{1}{1-\delta}\cdot\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(c(x,\xi_{i})-t)^{+}\right\} (4.1)

Sort the sample losses from worst to best as c[1]​(x)≥⋯≥c[n]​(x)c_{[1]}(x)\geq\cdots\geq c_{[n]}(x). The infimum over tt reduces to a weighted average of the upper tail, with m=⌈(1−δ)​n⌉m=\lceil(1-\delta)n\rceil:

CVaRδ,ξ∼F^n​[c⁡(x,ξ)]=11−δ⋅[1n⋅∑i=1m−1c[i]​(x)+(1−δ−m−1n)⋅c[m]​(x)].\text{CVaR}_{\delta,\xi\sim\hat{F}_{n}}\left[c\left(x,\xi\right)\right]\penalty\ \penalty\ =\penalty\ \penalty\ \frac{1}{1-\delta}\cdot\left[\frac{1}{n}\cdot\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}c_{[i]}\left(x\right)+\left(1-\delta-\frac{m-1}{n}\right)\cdot c_{[m]}\left(x\right)\right]\ .

An SAA action is a measurable minimizer

xSAA∈arg⁡minx∈𝒳​CVaRδ,ξ∼F^n​[c⁡(x,ξ)].x^{\mathrm{SAA}}\in\arg\min_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\text{CVaR}_{\delta,\xi\sim\hat{F}_{n}}[c(x,\xi)].

We assume a minimizer exists. If several actions attain it, xSAAx^{\mathrm{SAA}} is the one returned by a fixed measurable tie-break.

SAA minimizes an empirical estimate of the outcome-only objective QF​(⋅)Q_{F}\!\left(\cdot\right). The ex-ante value of the procedure is the CVaR of losses recorded across independent deployments, each with its own training sample. That is the object in which the sample-risk premium appears, and it is not the objective in equation (4.1).

4.1 Post-sample consistency and the sample-risk premium

Under the conditions below, the expected outcome-only CVaR of the action selected by SAA converges to the oracle benchmark. Thus the post-sample component in equation (3.3) vanishes.

Consistency and convergence-in-mean results are well established in SAA analysis; see, for example, Banholzer et al. (2022). The proposition below records a bounded, continuous setting in which expected post-sample regret vanishes, providing the starting point for analyzing the two components of combined-risk regret.

Proposition 4.1.

Fix a distribution FF. Suppose that:

  1. 1.

    The action set 𝒳\mathcal{X} is nonempty and compact.

  2. 2.

    The mapping x↦c⁡(x,ξ)x\mapsto c(x,\xi) is continuous on 𝒳\mathcal{X} for FF-almost every ξ\xi.

  3. 3.

    The loss is uniformly bounded under FF: there exists M<∞M<\infty such that

    supx∈𝒳|c⁡(x,ξ)|≤Malmost surely.\sup_{x\in\mathcal{X}}|c(x,\xi)|\leq M\qquad\text{almost surely}.

Then

PSδ,n​(πSAA,F)=𝔼ξ1n∼F​[QF​(xSAA)]−OPTδ​(F)⟶0.\mathrm{PS}_{\delta,n}(\pi^{\mathrm{SAA}},F)=\mathbb{E}_{\xi_{1}^{n}\sim F}\!\left[Q_{F}\!\left(x^{\mathrm{SAA}}\right)\right]-\text{OPT}_{\delta}(F)\longrightarrow 0.

The proof is in Appendix B. Proposition 4.1 controls the post-sample component. With several optimal actions, persistent mixing without a common minimizing threshold can still retain a positive premium, as Proposition 3.9 shows. If the oracle is unique, continuity on the compact action set makes it well separated, so Proposition 3.10 gives xSAA→xF∗x^{\mathrm{SAA}}\to x_{F}^{*} in probability. Boundedness and almost-sure continuity then give convergence of the induced losses in mean; continuity of CVaR in the L1L^{1} metric implies that combined-risk regret, and hence both components, vanish.

4.2 Concentration and regret rates

We next establish the concentration rate of SAA and determine how quickly each regret component vanishes. In addition to the structural conditions of the smooth or atomic regime, the rate uses almost-sure action differentiability at xF∗x_{F}^{*} and a local Lipschitz envelope with a moment above two. Specifically, ∂xc⁡(xF∗,ξ)\partial_{x}c(x_{F}^{*},\xi) exists for FF-almost every ξ\xi, and there is a nonnegative μ⁡(ξ)\mu(\xi) with 𝔼⁡[μ​(ξ)2+η]<∞\mathbb{E}[\mu(\xi)^{2+\eta}]<\infty for some η>0\eta>0 such that, for FF-almost every ξ\xi, simultaneously for all x,yx,y in a fixed neighborhood of xF∗x_{F}^{*},

|c⁡(x,ξ)−c⁡(y,ξ)|≤μ⁡(ξ)​|x−y|.\bigl|c(x,\xi)-c(y,\xi)\bigr|\penalty\ \penalty\ \leq\penalty\ \penalty\ \mu(\xi)\,|x-y|. (4.2)

These conditions control fluctuations of the empirical criterion near the oracle. For the squared loss (x−ξ)2(x-\xi)^{2} on a compact action interval, the derivative exists and one may take μ⁡(ξ)=C⁡(1+|ξ|)\mu(\xi)=C(1+|\xi|) for a suitable constant CC. Bounded outcomes also ensure the uniform loss bound in Proposition 4.1 and all required moments. The unbounded families in Table 1 provide values of KK; applying the SAA result below additionally requires its bounded-loss hypothesis.

Proposition 4.2.

Suppose the hypotheses of Proposition 4.1, and let xF∗x_{F}^{*} be the unique interior, well-separated oracle action. Assume the hypotheses on QFQ_{F}, the cutoff, and the loss distribution in either Theorem 3.4 or Theorem 3.5. Suppose also that the loss satisfies (4.2) with 𝔼⁡[μ​(ξ)2+η]<∞\mathbb{E}[\mu(\xi)^{2+\eta}]<\infty for some η>0\eta>0, and that ∂xc⁡(xF∗,ξ)\partial_{x}c(x_{F}^{*},\xi) exists for FF-almost every ξ\xi.

Write q∗=qF​(xF∗)q^{*}=q_{F}(x_{F}^{*}) and let aF=qF′​(xF∗)a_{F}=q_{F}^{\prime}(x_{F}^{*}) in the smooth regime and aF=ℓ′​(xF∗)a_{F}=\ell^{\prime}(x_{F}^{*}) in the atomic regime. Define

ψF​(ξ)=aF+∂xc⁡(xF∗,ξ)−aF1−δ𝟏{c(xF∗,ξ)>q∗},σ2=Var⁡(ψF​(ξ))QF′′​(xF∗)2.\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \psi_{F}(\xi)&=a_{F}+\frac{\partial_{x}c(x_{F}^{*},\xi)-a_{F}}{1-\delta}\mathbf{1}_{\{c(x_{F}^{*},\xi)>q^{*}\}},\\ \sigma^{2}&=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(\psi_{F}(\xi))}{Q_{F}^{\prime\prime}(x_{F}^{*})^{2}}.\end{aligned} (4.3)

Then 0<σ2<∞0<\sigma^{2}<\infty, and

n​(xSAA−xF∗)⇒𝒩⁡(0,σ2).\displaystyle\sqrt{n}\,(x^{\mathrm{SAA}}-x_{F}^{*})\ \Rightarrow\ \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}).

Moreover, {n​(xSAA−xF∗)2}n≥1\{n(x^{\mathrm{SAA}}-x_{F}^{*})^{2}\}_{n\geq 1} is uniformly integrable. In particular,

xSAA−xF∗=Θℙ(n−1/2).x^{\mathrm{SAA}}-x_{F}^{*}\penalty\ \penalty\ =\penalty\ \penalty\ \Theta_{\mathbb{P}}\!\left(n^{-1/2}\right).

The proof is in Appendix C. The normal limit and uniform integrability establish the concentration and moment conditions in Section 3 with rn=n−1/2r_{n}=n^{-1/2}. Bounded loss supplies the remainder estimates needed in the proofs of Theorems 3.4 and 3.5, giving

Smooth:PS=Θ(n−1),SR=Θ(n−1),Atomic:PS=Θ(n−1),SR=Θ(n−1/2).\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \text{Smooth:}\quad&\mathrm{PS}=\Theta(n^{-1}),\qquad\mathrm{SR}=\Theta(n^{-1}),\\ \text{Atomic:}\quad&\mathrm{PS}=\Theta(n^{-1}),\qquad\mathrm{SR}=\Theta(n^{-1/2}).\end{aligned}

The action converges at the same rate in both regimes, but combined-risk regret decays more slowly in the atomic regime because of the premium. In the smooth regime, the centered normal limit also gives ρn→K\rho_{n}\to K by Corollary 3.7.

The newsvendor loss is piecewise linear in the order with uniformly bounded slopes, so μ\mu can be chosen as a deterministic constant. Continuous demand makes the action derivative exist almost surely at the oracle and yields the isolation limits (Besbes and Rieger 2026). On a compact order set with bounded continuous demand, the proposition therefore applies when the structural atomic conditions of Theorem 3.5 hold.

4.3 Finite-sample illustrations

We evaluate SAA at finite sample sizes in two smooth squared-loss examples and an atomic newsvendor example.

Smooth losses.

Consider c⁡(x,ξ)=(ξ−x)2/2c(x,\xi)=(\xi-x)^{2}/2 at δ=0.95\delta=0.95, with 𝒳=[0,B]\mathcal{X}=[0,B]. The outcome is either exponential with rate 11, conditioned on ξ≤12\xi\leq 12, or lognormal with log⁡ξ∼𝒩⁡(0,1.82)\log\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1.8^{2}) before conditioning on ξ≤2000\xi\leq 2000; in each case BB is the upper bound. These bounded examples satisfy Proposition 4.2, as verified in Appendix C.2. Table 3 reports estimates from 12,00012{,}000 independent training samples for each row. Conditional risk evaluations use analytic truncated moments of the specified outcome distribution.

The estimated premium share ranges from 74.4%74.4\% to 93.5%93.5\% across these cases. Yet the finite-sample ratios remain below KK, especially for the lognormal outcome: at n=1600n=1600, the estimated ratio is 14.3814.38, compared with a limit of 418.42418.42. Thus the premium can already account for most regret while its ratio to post-sample regret is far from its local asymptotic value.

An atom at the cutoff.

Consider the newsvendor loss c⁡(x,ξ)=x/2−min⁡(x,ξ)c(x,\xi)=x/2-\min(x,\xi), with ξ∼U⁡[0,1]\xi\sim U[0,1], 𝒳=[0,1]\mathcal{X}=[0,1], and δ=0.9\delta=0.9. The unique oracle order is xF∗=0.05x_{F}^{*}=0.05, and the problem satisfies the atomic hypotheses. With the smallest-minimizer tie-break, SAA returns an order with exact sampling distribution

xSAA=ξ(k),k=⌈n/20⌉,ξ(k)∼Beta⁡(k,n+1−k).\displaystyle x^{\mathrm{SAA}}=\xi_{(k)},\qquad k=\lceil n/20\rceil,\qquad\xi_{(k)}\sim\operatorname{Beta}(k,n+1-k). (4.4)

Table 4 evaluates both regret components using this distribution. The premium accounts for about 76%76\% of regret at n=110n=110 and 95%95\% at n=1630n=1630. The scaled components approach the constants predicted by Propositions 4.2 and 3.8. Appendix C.3 gives the formulas and verifies the assumptions.

5 Conclusion

This paper studies an ex-ante notion of tail risk for data-driven decisions. We evaluate CVaR over the combined randomness of training, policy randomization, and the future outcome, relative to an oracle that knows the distribution. The resulting combined-risk regret decomposes into two nonnegative terms: average post-sample regret and a sample-risk premium. The first averages the outcome-only CVaR gaps of the selected actions; it already captures how learning affects action quality. The second measures the additional tail risk omitted by this averaging. This premium can be positive even when every selected action is individually optimal under outcome-only CVaR.

The regime analysis shows how the premium can become the main component of regret. Under the smooth-regime hypotheses, the two components have the same asymptotic order. For centered limiting fluctuations, the ratio of the premium to post-sample regret tends to KK, which can be large. The curvature comparison explains this difference: using one tail threshold across samples adds a variance penalty. The limit alone does not determine the ratio at a given sample size. Under the atomic-regime hypotheses, the premium decays more slowly than average post-sample regret and becomes the leading component. With persistent mixing among optimal actions that admit no common minimizing threshold, the premium can remain positive even as average post-sample regret vanishes.

Sample average approximation illustrates the distinction between action convergence and regret. Under Proposition 4.2, its action converges at rate n−1/2n^{-1/2} in both the smooth and atomic regimes, but its combined-risk regret is of order n−1n^{-1} in the first and n−1/2n^{-1/2} in the second. The finite-sample examples in Tables 3 and 4 illustrate the importance of the premium in both regimes: it accounts for approximately 74%74\%–97%97\% of regret in the reported cases. In the smooth examples, these large premium shares occur while the ratios remain below their limiting coefficients.

These regimes are representative settings at a fixed distribution, not an exhaustive classification. The smooth expansion also identifies a local design tradeoff: at leading order, action variance receives weight 1+K1+K relative to squared bias. Comparing policies through this expansion requires both to satisfy its hypotheses. Finite-sample guarantees for policy changes motivated by this tradeoff, and statistical guarantees for estimating KK and the cutoff-based upper bound, remain questions for further work. Evaluating a learned policy through its average outcome-only risk can omit a leading component of excess tail risk.

Appendix A Decomposition of regret

A.1 Proof of Proposition 3.2

For x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} and t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}, write ϕx​(t):=ϕF​(x,t)\phi_{x}(t):=\phi_{F}\!\left(x,t\right), so that

QF​(x)=mint∈ℝ⁡ϕx​(t),𝒯δ​(x)=arg⁡mint∈ℝ​ϕx​(t).Q_{F}\!\left(x\right)=\min_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\phi_{x}(t),\qquad\mathcal{T}_{\delta}(x)=\arg\min_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\phi_{x}(t).

Both the minimum and the minimizing set are nonempty for almost every realization of xπx^{\pi}, by integrability.

Part 1.

By the independence of xπx^{\pi} and ξ\xi and equation (3.4),

SRδ,n​(π,F)=inft∈ℝG⁡(t),G⁡(t):=𝔼xπ​[ϕxπ​(t)−mins∈ℝ⁡ϕxπ​(s)],\mathrm{SR}_{\delta,n}\!\left(\pi,F\right)=\inf_{t\in\mathbb{R}}G(t),\qquad G(t):=\mathbb{E}_{x^{\pi}}\!\left[\phi_{x^{\pi}}(t)-\min_{s\in\mathbb{R}}\phi_{x^{\pi}}(s)\right],

and the integrand defining G⁡(t)G(t) is nonnegative for every tt. The quantity 𝔼xπ​[mins⁡ϕxπ​(s)]=𝔼xπ​[QF​(xπ)]\mathbb{E}_{x^{\pi}}[\min_{s}\phi_{x^{\pi}}(s)]=\mathbb{E}_{x^{\pi}}[Q_{F}\!\left(x^{\pi}\right)] is finite by integrability and does not depend on tt, so GG differs from t↦𝔼xπ​[ϕxπ​(t)]t\mapsto\mathbb{E}_{x^{\pi}}[\phi_{x^{\pi}}(t)] by a constant. Consequently GG attains its infimum at any t∗t^{*} attaining the variational representation of CVaRδ​[c⁡(xπ,ξ)]\text{CVaR}_{\delta}[c(x^{\pi},\xi)], and such a t∗t^{*} exists by integrability.

Suppose first that the tails are aligned, so that some t⋆t^{\star} satisfies t⋆∈𝒯δ​(xπ)t^{\star}\in\mathcal{T}_{\delta}(x^{\pi}) almost surely. Then ϕxπ​(t⋆)=mins⁡ϕxπ​(s)\phi_{x^{\pi}}(t^{\star})=\min_{s}\phi_{x^{\pi}}(s) almost surely, hence G⁡(t⋆)=0G(t^{\star})=0 and the premium vanishes. Conversely, suppose the premium vanishes, so that G⁡(t∗)=0G(t^{*})=0. The integrand is nonnegative, whence ϕxπ​(t∗)=mins⁡ϕxπ​(s)\phi_{x^{\pi}}(t^{*})=\min_{s}\phi_{x^{\pi}}(s) almost surely, that is, t∗∈𝒯δ​(xπ)t^{*}\in\mathcal{T}_{\delta}(x^{\pi}) almost surely, and the tails are aligned. Finally, if xπ=x0x^{\pi}=x_{0} almost surely, then any element of 𝒯δ​(x0)\mathcal{T}_{\delta}(x_{0}), a nonempty set, serves as a common threshold; the tails are aligned and the premium vanishes.

Part 2.

By definition,

PSδ,n​(π,F)=𝔼xπ​[QF​(xπ)]−OPTδ​(F)=𝔼xπ​[QF​(xπ)−OPTδ​(F)],\mathrm{PS}_{\delta,n}\!\left(\pi,F\right)=\mathbb{E}_{x^{\pi}}\!\left[Q_{F}\!\left(x^{\pi}\right)\right]-\text{OPT}_{\delta}(F)=\mathbb{E}_{x^{\pi}}\!\left[Q_{F}\!\left(x^{\pi}\right)-\text{OPT}_{\delta}(F)\right],

and QF​(x)≥OPTδ​(F)Q_{F}\!\left(x\right)\geq\text{OPT}_{\delta}(F) for every x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, so the integrand is nonnegative. Hence PSδ,n​(π,F)=0\mathrm{PS}_{\delta,n}\!\left(\pi,F\right)=0 if and only if QF​(xπ)=OPTδ​(F)Q_{F}\!\left(x^{\pi}\right)=\text{OPT}_{\delta}(F) almost surely. Since the infimum defining OPTδ​(F)\text{OPT}_{\delta}(F) is attained, {x∈𝒳:QF​(x)=OPTδ​(F)}=𝒳F∗\{x\in\mathcal{X}:Q_{F}\!\left(x\right)=\text{OPT}_{\delta}(F)\}=\mathcal{X}^{*}_{F}, so this is exactly xπ∈𝒳F∗x^{\pi}\in\mathcal{X}^{*}_{F} almost surely. If the oracle action is unique, 𝒳F∗={xF∗}\mathcal{X}^{*}_{F}=\{x^{*}_{F}\} and the condition reads xπ=xF∗x^{\pi}=x^{*}_{F} almost surely.

A.2 Proof of Proposition 3.3

Write Y=qF​(xπ)Y=q_{F}(x^{\pi}). Markov’s inequality gives

|qF​(x)|≤𝔼ξ​|c⁡(x,ξ)|min⁡{δ,1−δ},|q_{F}(x)|\leq\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\xi}|c(x,\xi)|}{\min\{\delta,1-\delta\}},

so YY is integrable. The one-sided threshold derivatives of ϕF​(x,t)\phi_{F}(x,t) lie in [−δ/(1−δ),1][-\delta/(1-\delta),1]. Since qF​(x)q_{F}(x) minimizes this convex function,

0≤ϕF​(x,t)−QF​(x)≤(t−qF​(x))++δ1−δ​(qF​(x)−t)+.0\leq\phi_{F}(x,t)-Q_{F}(x)\leq(t-q_{F}(x))^{+}+\frac{\delta}{1-\delta}(q_{F}(x)-t)^{+}.

Taking expectations and infima in tt, and using the CVaR variational formula, gives

0≤SR\displaystyle 0\leq\mathrm{SR} ≤inft𝔼⁡[(t−Y)++δ1−δ​(Y−t)+]\displaystyle\leq\inf_{t}\mathbb{E}\left[(t-Y)^{+}+\frac{\delta}{1-\delta}(Y-t)^{+}\right]
=inft{t+𝔼⁡[(Y−t)+]1−δ}−𝔼​Y=CVaRδ​[Y]−𝔼​Y.\displaystyle=\inf_{t}\left\{t+\frac{\mathbb{E}[(Y-t)^{+}]}{1-\delta}\right\}-\mathbb{E}Y=\text{CVaR}_{\delta}[Y]-\mathbb{E}Y.

For a conditionally deterministic loss, QF​(x)=qF​(x)=c⁡(x,ξ)Q_{F}(x)=q_{F}(x)=c(x,\xi) almost surely, so SR=CVaRδ​[Y]−𝔼​Y\mathrm{SR}=\text{CVaR}_{\delta}[Y]-\mathbb{E}Y. Since Lδ=max⁡{1,δ/(1−δ)}L_{\delta}=\max\{1,\delta/(1-\delta)\},

(t−Y)++δ1−δ​(Y−t)+≤Lδ​|Y−t|.(t-Y)^{+}+\frac{\delta}{1-\delta}(Y-t)^{+}\leq L_{\delta}|Y-t|.

Taking the expectation and the infimum in tt gives the last inequality in equation (3.5).

A.3 A linear rate from the premium bound

Corollary A.1 (Linear rate for the sample-risk premium).

Maintain the hypotheses of Proposition 3.3 and the Lipschitz condition (2.6). Let x∗x^{*} be such that qFq_{F} is differentiable at x∗x^{*}, and suppose xπ=x∗+rn​Znx^{\pi}=x^{*}+r_{n}Z_{n} with rn→0r_{n}\to 0 and supn𝔼​|Zn|<∞\sup_{n}\mathbb{E}|Z_{n}|<\infty. Then SR=O⁡(rn)\mathrm{SR}=O(r_{n}).

Proof.

Differentiability at x∗x^{*} gives |qF​(x)−qF​(x∗)|≤C​|x−x∗||q_{F}(x)-q_{F}(x^{*})|\leq C|x-x^{*}| in a fixed neighborhood. The Lipschitz envelope in (2.6) and Markov’s inequality in the proof of Proposition 3.3 give |qF​(x)−qF​(x∗)|≤C′​(1+|x−x∗|)|q_{F}(x)-q_{F}(x^{*})|\leq C^{\prime}(1+|x-x^{*}|) globally. Outside that neighborhood the same comparison is bounded by a constant times |x−x∗||x-x^{*}|. Evaluating (3.5) at t=qF​(x∗)t=q_{F}(x^{*}) therefore gives

SR≤C′′​𝔼​|xπ−x∗|=C′′​rn​𝔼​|Zn|=O⁡(rn).\mathrm{SR}\leq C^{\prime\prime}\mathbb{E}|x^{\pi}-x^{*}|=C^{\prime\prime}r_{n}\mathbb{E}|Z_{n}|=O(r_{n}).

∎

A.4 Proof of Theorem 3.4

Both PSδ,n​(π,F)\mathrm{PS}_{\delta,n}\!\left(\pi,F\right) and SRδ,n​(π,F)\mathrm{SR}_{\delta,n}\!\left(\pi,F\right) are expectations, and the hypotheses control them near x∗x^{*}. The argument records that local control and the orders it induces, and then checks that the contribution of the event on which the induced action leaves a neighborhood of x∗x^{*} is o⁡(rn2)o(r_{n}^{2}).

Twice differentiability of QFQ_{F} at the interior minimizer x∗x^{*}, with 0<QF′′​(x∗)<∞0<Q_{F}^{\prime\prime}(x^{*})<\infty, makes QF​(x)−QF​(x∗)Q_{F}\!\left(x\right)-Q_{F}\!\left(x^{*}\right) quadratic in |x−x∗||x-x^{*}|. The assumption qF′​(x∗)≠0q_{F}^{\prime}(x^{*})\neq 0 makes the cutoff move linearly with the action. A positive finite density of the loss, continuous at (x∗,q∗)(x^{*},q^{*}), makes the variational objective from equation (2.3) quadratic in the threshold. The following lemma turns those facts into bounds on a neighborhood of x∗x^{*}: the outcome-only CVaR grows like |x−x∗|2|x-x^{*}|^{2}, the cutoff moves linearly with the action, and the variational objective grows like the square of the distance from the cutoff.

|qF​(x)−q∗−qF′​(x∗)​(x−x∗)|\displaystyle\left|\,q_{F}\!\left(x\right)-q^{*}-q_{F}^{\prime}(x^{*})\left(x-x^{*}\right)\,\right|\penalty\ \penalty\ ≤ε​|x−x∗|,\displaystyle\leq\penalty\ \penalty\ \varepsilon\left|x-x^{*}\right|\ , (A.2)

Lemma A.3 (Orders under local brackets).
