A.5 Proof of Lemma A.3

The comparisons in equations (A.1)–(A.3) bound a fixed action. The post-sample regret is the expectation of QF​(xπ)−QF​(x∗)Q_{F}\!\left(x^{\pi}\right)-Q_{F}\!\left(x^{*}\right), so on the event A:={xπ∈𝒩}A:=\{x^{\pi}\in\mathcal{N}\} the first comparison bounds it by a second moment of Δ:=xπ−x∗\Delta:=x^{\pi}-x^{*}, and the contribution of AcA^{c} is a remainder. The premium is the price of one shared threshold against the action-specific cutoffs qF​(xπ)q_{F}\!\left(x^{\pi}\right), so on AA it is the distance from qF​(xπ)q_{F}\!\left(x^{\pi}\right) to a single constant. For γ≥1\gamma\geq 1, a random variable WW and an event AA, let

𝒟γ​(W,A):=inft∈ℝ𝔼⁡[|W−t|γ​𝟏A],\mathcal{D}_{\gamma}\!\left(W\,;\,A\right)\penalty\ \penalty\ :=\penalty\ \penalty\ \inf_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left|W-t\right|^{\gamma}\mathbf{1}_{A}\right]\ , (A.7)

and write 𝒟γ​(W)\mathcal{D}_{\gamma}\!\left(W\right) when AA is the sure event. This is the best approximation of WW by a single constant, measured in γ\gamma-th absolute moment. For γ=2\gamma=2 it is the variance, attained at the mean; for γ=1\gamma=1 it is the mean absolute deviation about the median. The functional is invariant under deterministic shifts,

𝒟γ​(W+b,A)=𝒟γ​(W,A)for every constant ​b,\mathcal{D}_{\gamma}\!\left(W+b\,;\,A\right)\penalty\ \penalty\ =\penalty\ \penalty\ \mathcal{D}_{\gamma}\!\left(W\,;\,A\right)\qquad\text{for every constant }b\ ,

and it vanishes precisely when WW is almost surely constant on AA.

The expansion of the cutoff carries the distance for qF​(xπ)q_{F}\!\left(x^{\pi}\right) over to the same distance for Δ\Delta. The resulting bounds hold at a single sample size, and the orders are obtained by scaling them once the remainders are of smaller order. The next lemma records both bounds and this transfer. The exponent γ≥1\gamma\geq 1 is free: the smooth regime takes γ=2\gamma=2, and the atomic regime takes γ=1\gamma=1.

An elementary observation.

The one estimate the fixed-nn lemma does not supply is that a dispersion functional cannot degenerate along a weakly convergent sequence. Fix γ≥1\gamma\geq 1 and let Yn⇒YY_{n}\Rightarrow Y with {|Yn|γ}\{|Y_{n}|^{\gamma}\} uniformly integrable and YY nondegenerate. Then

0<lim infn→∞𝒟γ​(Yn)≤lim supn→∞𝒟γ​(Yn)<∞.0<\liminf_{n\to\infty}\mathcal{D}_{\gamma}\!\left(Y_{n}\right)\leq\limsup_{n\to\infty}\mathcal{D}_{\gamma}\!\left(Y_{n}\right)<\infty. (A.12)

If the lower bound failed, there would exist tnt_{n} with 𝔼⁡[|Yn−tn|γ]→0\mathbb{E}[|Y_{n}-t_{n}|^{\gamma}]\to 0. Restricting the functional to a high-probability event cannot destroy this, and the resulting bound is uniform in the event, which is what lets a radius be chosen below without circularity. Let {En}\{E_{n}\} be any events with ℙ⁡(En)→1\mathbb{P}(E_{n})\to 1. Then

A.6 Proof of Lemma A.4

Throughout write x∗:=xF∗x^{*}:=x^{*}_{F}, q∗:=qF​(x∗)q^{*}:=q_{F}\!\left(x^{*}\right), Δ:=xπ−x∗\Delta:=x^{\pi}-x^{*} and A:={xπ∈𝒩}A:=\{x^{\pi}\in\mathcal{N}\}. For a fixed action xx set

hx​(u):=ϕF​(x,qF​(x)+u)−QF​(x).h_{x}(u)\penalty\ :=\penalty\ \phi_{F}\!\left(x,q_{F}\!\left(x\right)+u\right)-Q_{F}\!\left(x\right)\ .

Since (c⁡(x,ξ)−t)+(c(x,\xi)-t)^{+} is convex in tt, the map t↦ϕF​(x,t)t\mapsto\phi_{F}\!\left(x,t\right) is convex, and hence so is hxh_{x}. By definition of qF​(x)q_{F}\!\left(x\right) as a minimizer, hx≥0=hx​(0)h_{x}\geq 0=h_{x}(0). A convex function attaining its minimum at the origin is nonincreasing on (−∞,0](-\infty,0] and nondecreasing on [0,∞)[0,\infty), so |u|↦hx​(u)|u|\mapsto h_{x}(u) is nondecreasing on each side of the origin. We use this monotonicity twice below. If ℙ⁡(A)=0\mathbb{P}(A)=0 the terms supported on AA vanish, and the inequalities reduce to the remainder bounds 0≤PSδ,n​(π,F)≤RPS0\leq\mathrm{PS}_{\delta,n}\!\left(\pi,F\right)\leq R_{\mathrm{PS}} and 0≤SRδ,n​(π,F)≤RSR0\leq\mathrm{SR}_{\delta,n}\!\left(\pi,F\right)\leq R_{\mathrm{SR}}. Assume ℙ⁡(A)>0\mathbb{P}(A)>0.

Geometry of the neighborhood.

Comparing the two bounds in (A.3) at any u≠0u\neq 0 gives cγ≤Cγc_{\gamma}\leq C_{\gamma}. The radius condition (A.8) keeps every induced cutoff inside the interval on which those bounds apply. Its right-hand side is at most u0/4u_{0}/4. Set κ:=(|qF′​(x∗)|+ε)​η\kappa:=(|q_{F}^{\prime}(x^{*})|+\varepsilon)\eta. By the VaR\mathrm{VaR} expansion (A.2), for every x∈𝒩x\in\mathcal{N},

A.17 Proof of Proposition 3.9

The proof proceeds by coupling xπx^{\pi} with its weak limit. Continuity and uniform integrability then imply L1L^{1} convergence of the induced losses. The L1L^{1} continuity of CVaR allows us to pass both terms in the regret decomposition to the limit, after which the strict positivity result follows from Lemma A.8 below.

Convergence of the induced losses.

By the Skorokhod representation theorem, we may construct random variables xnπx_{n}^{\pi} and x∞πx_{\infty}^{\pi} with the same respective distributions as xπx^{\pi} and x∞πx_{\infty}^{\pi} such that

xnπ⟶x∞πalmost surely.x_{n}^{\pi}\longrightarrow x_{\infty}^{\pi}\qquad\text{almost surely}.

Let ξ∼F\xi\sim F be independent of (xnπ,x∞π)(x_{n}^{\pi},x_{\infty}^{\pi}). By the assumed continuity of x↦c⁡(x,ξ)x\mapsto c(x,\xi) at x∞πx_{\infty}^{\pi},

c⁡(xnπ,ξ)⟶c⁡(x∞π,ξ)almost surely.c(x_{n}^{\pi},\xi)\longrightarrow c(x_{\infty}^{\pi},\xi)\qquad\text{almost surely}.

The family {|c⁡(xnπ,ξ)|}n≥1\{|c(x_{n}^{\pi},\xi)|\}_{n\geq 1} is uniformly integrable because xnπx_{n}^{\pi} has the same distribution as xπx^{\pi}. Hence, by uniform integrability,

𝔼⁡[|c⁡(xnπ,ξ)−c⁡(x∞π,ξ)|]⟶0.\mathbb{E}\left[|c(x_{n}^{\pi},\xi)-c(x_{\infty}^{\pi},\xi)|\right]\longrightarrow 0. (A.24)

For integrable random variables YY and Y′Y^{\prime},

|CVaRδ​[Y]−CVaRδ​[Y′]|≤11−δ​𝔼​|Y−Y′|.|\text{CVaR}_{\delta}[Y]-\text{CVaR}_{\delta}[Y^{\prime}]|\leq\frac{1}{1-\delta}\mathbb{E}|Y-Y^{\prime}|.

Applying this inequality conditionally on (xnπ,x∞π)(x_{n}^{\pi},x_{\infty}^{\pi}) and then taking expectations, (A.24) gives

𝔼⁡[|CVaRδ,ξ∼F​[c⁡(xnπ,ξ)]−CVaRδ,ξ∼F​[c⁡(x∞π,ξ)]|]⟶0.\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left|\text{CVaR}_{\delta,\xi\sim F}[c(x_{n}^{\pi},\xi)]-\text{CVaR}_{\delta,\xi\sim F}[c(x_{\infty}^{\pi},\xi)]\right|\right]\longrightarrow 0.

Since x∞πx_{\infty}^{\pi} is supported on population-optimal actions,

CVaRδ,ξ∼F​[c⁡(x∞π,ξ)]=OPTδ​(F)almost surely.\text{CVaR}_{\delta,\xi\sim F}[c(x_{\infty}^{\pi},\xi)]=\text{OPT}_{\delta}(F)\qquad\text{almost surely}.

PSδ,n​(π,F)⟶0.\mathrm{PS}_{\delta,n}(\pi,F)\longrightarrow 0.

Applying the same L1L^{1} continuity of CVaR directly to (A.24) yields

CVaRδ,xnπ,ξ​[c⁡(xnπ,ξ)]⟶CVaRδ,x∞π,ξ​[c⁡(x∞π,ξ)].\text{CVaR}_{\delta,x_{n}^{\pi},\xi}[c(x_{n}^{\pi},\xi)]\longrightarrow\text{CVaR}_{\delta,x_{\infty}^{\pi},\xi}[c(x_{\infty}^{\pi},\xi)].

Together with the preceding convergence of the expected outcome-only CVaR, this implies

SRδ,n​(π,F)⟶CVaRδ,x∞π,ξ​[c⁡(x∞π,ξ)]−𝔼x∞π​[CVaRδ,ξ∼F​[c⁡(x∞π,ξ)]]=:SRδ,∞​(π,F).\mathrm{SR}_{\delta,n}(\pi,F)\longrightarrow\text{CVaR}_{\delta,x_{\infty}^{\pi},\xi}[c(x_{\infty}^{\pi},\xi)]-\mathbb{E}_{x_{\infty}^{\pi}}\!\left[\text{CVaR}_{\delta,\xi\sim F}[c(x_{\infty}^{\pi},\xi)]\right]=:\mathrm{SR}_{\delta,\infty}(\pi,F).

The limit is the sample-risk premium of the limiting action. The same comparison holds for any integrable action independent of the future outcome, so the strict inequality is recorded on its own.

Lemma A.8.

Under the hypotheses of Proposition 3.2, if the conditional tails induced by xπx^{\pi} are misaligned, then

C.1 Proof of Proposition 4.2 and the regret rates

Lemma C.2 gives the normal limit, uniform integrability, and the stated rate in probability.

The normal limit and uniform integrability give (3.6) with rn=n−1/2r_{n}=n^{-1/2}. For a fixed action neighborhood An={|Δn|≤r}A_{n}=\{|\Delta_{n}|\leq r\}, uniform integrability implies

n​ℙ​(Anc)≤r−2​𝔼​[n​Δn2​𝟏Anc]⟶0.n\mathbb{P}(A_{n}^{c})\leq r^{-2}\mathbb{E}[n\Delta_{n}^{2}\mathbf{1}_{A_{n}^{c}}]\longrightarrow 0.

Bounded loss gives |QF​(x)−QF​(x∗)|≤2​M|Q_{F}(x)-Q_{F}(x^{*})|\leq 2M and |qF​(x)|≤M|q_{F}(x)|\leq M. The escape remainders in Lemma A.3 are therefore O⁡(ℙ⁡(Anc))=o⁡(n−1)O(\mathbb{P}(A_{n}^{c}))=o(n^{-1}). The proofs of Theorems 3.4 and 3.5 apply with these bounds replacing the global Lipschitz estimates for those remainders. They give PS,SR=Θ⁡(n−1)\mathrm{PS},\mathrm{SR}=\Theta(n^{-1}) in the smooth regime, and PS=Θ⁡(n−1)\mathrm{PS}=\Theta(n^{-1}), SR=Θ(n−1/2)\mathrm{SR}=\Theta(n^{-1/2}) in the atomic regime. The same replacement applies to the coefficient limits in Propositions 3.6 and 3.8 and hence to Corollary 3.7 in the smooth regime.

For each outcome distribution and n∈{100,400,1600}n\in\{100,400,1600\}, generate R=12,000R=12{,}000 independent training samples and compute their SAA actions x1SAA,…,xRSAAx_{1}^{\mathrm{SAA}},\ldots,x_{R}^{\mathrm{SAA}}.
